Explore a comprehensive list of discourse probing tasks as an alternative method.
papers.abstract: While a large body of literature suggests that large language models (LLMs) acquire rich linguistic representations, little is known about whether they adapt to linguistic biases in a human-like way. The present study probes this question by asking whether LLMs display human-like referential biases using stimuli and procedures from real psycholinguistic experiments. Recent psycholinguistic studies suggest that humans adapt their referential biases with recent exposure to referential patterns; closely replicating three relevant psycholinguistic experiments from Johnson & Arnold (2022) in an in-context learning (ICL) framework, we found that InstructGPT adapts its pronominal interpretations in response to the frequency of referential patterns in the local discourse, though in a limited fashion: adaptation was only observed relative to syntactic but not semantic biases. By contrast, FLAN-UL2 fails to generate meaningful patterns. Our results provide further evidence that contemporary LLMs discourse representations are sensitive to syntactic patterns in the local context but less so to semantic patterns. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/zkx06111/llm_priming.

papers.title: Improving Activation Steering in Language Models with Mean-Centring
papers.research_question: How can activation steering in language models be improved by applying mean-centring to steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Mean-centring, a simple post-processing step that subtracts the mean of training activations from the mean of target activations, creates more effective steering vectors for activation steering, improving performance and applicability.
papers.conclusion: Mean-centring is a simple and effective technique that improves activation steering by accounting for anisotropy in model activations, making it applicable to a wider range of tasks where counterbalancing concepts are not available.
papers.key_findings:
Mean-centring produces more interpretable and effective steering vectors compared to using raw activation averages.
Mean-centring is effective for reducing toxicity in model outputs, comparable to existing methods like ActAdd.
Mean-centring can steer story continuations towards a target genre, increasing genre-specific word frequencies.
Mean-centring significantly improves the accuracy of function vectors for triggering tasks like country-capital and English-French translation.
papers.limitation:
Mean-centring does not improve performance at all layers of the model.
The link between anisotropy (as measured by average cosine similarity) and the performance improvement from mean-centring is not clearly predictive.
future_direction: Investigating the link between anisotropy and improvements in accuracy from mean-centring.
Investigating other structures in activation geometries (e.g., clustering) for further improvements to steering.
papers.abstract: Recent work in activation steering has demonstrated the potential to better control the outputs of Large Language Models (LLMs), but it involves finding steering vectors. This is difficult because engineers do not typically know how features are represented in these models. We seek to address this issue by applying the idea of mean-centring to steering vectors. We find that taking the average of activations associated with a target dataset, and then subtracting the mean of all training activations, results in effective steering vectors. We test this method on a variety of models on natural language tasks by steering away from generating toxic text, and steering the completion of a story towards a target genre. We also apply mean-centring to extract function vectors, more effectively triggering the execution of a range of natural language tasks by a significant margin (compared to previous baselines). This suggests that mean-centring can be used to easily improve the effectiveness of activation steering in a wide range of contexts.

papers.title: Identifying and Adapting Transformer-Components Responsible for Gender Bias in an English Language Model
papers.research_question: Where in a given language model is gender bias introduced, and can this information be used to mitigate bias effectively?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DiffMask+, an efficient method for identifying transformer components causally responsible for gender bias, and demonstrates that fine-tuning only these components can mitigate bias with minimal degradation to general language modeling performance.
papers.conclusion: The work provides an exploratory study showing that causal methods can identify components responsible for gender bias, and that targeted, parameter-efficient fine-tuning of these components can mitigate bias while largely preserving language modeling capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Three causal discovery methods (CMA, ACDC, DiffMask+) identify largely overlapping sets of attention heads, primarily in the last four layers of GPT-2 small, as responsible for gender bias.
Fine-tuning only the identified attention heads reduces gender bias on evaluation datasets (CrowS-Pairs, Professions) with less damage to perplexity and linguistic agreement tasks compared to full-model fine-tuning.
The new DiffMask+ method is computationally more efficient than automated circuit discovery (ACDC) for component identification.
The dataset used for causal discovery influences which components are identified, highlighting a sensitivity in the procedures.
Bias mitigation results vary across different evaluation datasets (e.g., CrowS-Pairs vs. WinoBias), underscoring challenges in defining and measuring bias.
papers.limitation:
The operationalization of gender bias uses minimal pairs of contrasting sentences, which simplifies gender as a binary construct and may not generalize well to other languages.
Causal discovery procedures are sensitive to the choice of dataset used for discovery.
Success in bias reduction varies across different bias evaluation benchmarks, indicating challenges in defining and measuring bias.
future_direction: Development of more reliable and validated bias measures.
More effective mitigation strategies for other types of bias.
Attention to dataset development for bias analysis.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) exhibit and amplify many types of undesirable biases learned from the training data, including gender bias. However, we lack tools for effectively and efficiently changing this behavior without hurting general language modeling performance. In this paper, we study three methods for identifying causal relations between LM components and particular output: causal mediation analysis, automated circuit discovery and our novel, efficient method called DiffMask+ based on differential masking. We apply the methods to GPT-2 small and the problem of gender bias, and use the discovered sets of components to perform parameter-efficient fine-tuning for bias mitigation. Our results show significant overlap in the identified components (despite huge differences in the computational requirements of the methods) as well as success in mitigating gender bias, with less damage to general language modeling compared to full model fine-tuning. However, our work also underscores the difficulty of defining and measuring bias, and the sensitivity of causal discovery procedures to dataset choice. We hope our work can contribute to more attention for dataset development, and lead to more effective mitigation strategies for other types of bias.

papers.title: Debiasing Algorithm through Model Adaptation
papers.research_question: Can we identify evidence of gender bias in LLaMA? Can we identify which components store the gender-biased representation? Can we edit the model's weights to decrease bias while preserving performance on end-tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DAMA, a method to debias language models by identifying bias-mediating components via causal tracing and editing their weights via linear projection, significantly reducing gender bias while preserving performance.
papers.conclusion: DAMA effectively reduces gender bias in LLaMA models by editing weights of bias-mediating MLP layers, with minimal impact on general language understanding and task performance.
papers.key_findings:
LLaMA models exhibit gender bias in language generation, coreference resolution, and sentence completion.
Mid-upper MLP layers are the primary mediators of gender bias in LLaMA models.
DAMA significantly reduces gender bias across multiple metrics (language generation, WinoBias, StereoSet).
DAMA maintains the model's performance on language modeling and downstream tasks (ARC, OBQA, MMLU) with minimal degradation.
The method is effective across different model sizes (7B, 13B, 30B, 65B).
papers.limitation: The method's effectiveness may depend on the choice of layers and projection dimensions, requiring hyperparameter tuning.
future_direction: Improve the method of finding projection matrices, possibly using convex search or analytically derived pseudo-projections.
Investigate further the ranges of layers and dimensions that convey bias to apply DAMA effectively on other model types.
Extend the approach to other languages, particularly morphologically rich languages with more ubiquitous gender marking.
papers.abstract: Large language models are becoming the go-to solution for the ever-growing number of tasks. However, with growing capacity, models are prone to rely on spurious correlations stemming from biases and stereotypes present in the training data. This work proposes a novel method for detecting and mitigating gender bias in language models. We perform causal analysis to identify problematic model components and discover that mid-upper feed-forward layers are most prone to convey bias. Based on the analysis results, we intervene in the model by applying a linear projection to the weight matrices of these layers. Our titular method, DAMA, significantly decreases bias as measured by diverse metrics while maintaining the model's performance on downstream tasks. We release code for our method and models, which retrain LLaMA's state-of-the-art performance while being significantly less biased.

papers.title: An Adversarial Example for Direct Logit Attribution: Memory Management in GELU-4L
papers.research_question: Does memory management (erasure) occur in transformers, and how does it affect the interpretation of model components via direct logit attribution?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides concrete evidence for memory management (erasure) in a 4-layer transformer and demonstrates that direct logit attribution (DLA) can yield misleading results when erasure is present.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight the need for caution when using DLA, as erasure can lead to misleading results. The authors recommend testing effects across varied prompts and complementing DLA with activation patching.
papers.key_findings:
The output of attention head L0H2 is erased by later attention heads in layer 2.
The erasure behavior is causally dependent on V-composition between the writing and erasing heads.
DLA contributions of the writing head and erasing heads are highly anti-correlated, indicating DLA can overstate the writing head's contribution.
Adversarial examples show high DLA values for the writing head even when its input is patched, indicating the DLA signal is not genuine.
papers.limitation: The study focused on a single model and a specific attention head, so the generalizability of the phenomena to other components and model sizes is unclear.
papers.abstract: Prior work suggests that language models manage the limited bandwidth of the residual stream through a "memory management" mechanism, where certain attention heads and MLP layers clear residual stream directions set by earlier layers. Our study provides concrete evidence for this erasure phenomenon in a 4-layer transformer, identifying heads that consistently remove the output of earlier heads. We further demonstrate that direct logit attribution (DLA), a common technique for interpreting the output of intermediate transformer layers, can show misleading results by not accounting for erasure.

papers.title: Investigating Bias Representations in Llama 2 Chat via Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How does activation steering reveal and mitigate societal biases in Llama 2 7B Chat, and what does this say about the model's internal representations of bias?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering uncovers inherent gender bias in Llama 2 7B Chat and shows that RLHF leads to increased similarity in the model's representation of different societal biases, suggesting a loss of nuanced understanding.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering is effective for red-teaming biases in LLMs, and RLHF may cause the model to conflate different bias types, reducing nuanced understanding.
papers.key_findings:
Llama 2 7B Chat exhibits inherent gender bias despite undergoing Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF).
Bias steering vectors trigger refusal responses, and subtracting a refusal vector can elicit biased outputs from the model.
Bias vectors are transferable across dimensions; for example, racial bias steering can elicit gender and religion bias.
There is a negative correlation between bias vectors and refusal vectors, as shown by cosine similarity across layers.
RLHF increases the cosine similarity between different bias vectors in the Chat model compared to the base model, indicating that biases become more closely associated.
papers.abstract: We address the challenge of societal bias in Large Language Models (LLMs), focusing on the Llama 2 7B Chat model. As LLMs are increasingly integrated into decision-making processes with substantial societal impact, it becomes imperative to ensure these models do not reinforce existing biases. Our approach employs activation steering to probe for and mitigate biases related to gender, race, and religion. This method manipulates model activations to direct responses towards or away from biased outputs, utilizing steering vectors derived from the StereoSet dataset and custom GPT4 generated gender bias prompts. Our findings reveal inherent gender bias in Llama 2 7B Chat, persisting even after Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). We also observe a predictable negative correlation between bias and the model's tendency to refuse responses. Significantly, our study uncovers that RLHF tends to increase the similarity in the model's representation of different forms of societal biases, which raises questions about the model's nuanced understanding of different forms of bias. This work also provides valuable insights into effective red-teaming strategies for LLMs using activation steering, particularly emphasizing the importance of integrating a refusal vector.

papers.title: Personalized Steering of Large Language Models: Versatile Steering Vectors Through Bi-directional Preference Optimization
papers.research_question: How can we produce more effective steering vectors for personalized control of LLMs, particularly in alignment-related scenarios?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Bi-directional Preference Optimization (BiPO) to compute effective steering vectors for LLMs, enabling personalized control of behaviors by adjusting vector direction and magnitude.
papers.conclusion: Proposes BiPO for effective steering vectors, enabling personalized behavior control without additional training, with demonstrated versatility and transferability.
papers.key_findings:
BiPO outperforms baseline methods (CAA and Freeform) in steering AI personas, as measured by behavioral scores.
BiPO effectively steers models in alignment-related scenarios, including truthfulness, hallucination, and jailbreaking attacks and defenses.
The optimized steering vectors are transferable across different models (e.g., from Llama-2 to Vicuna) and fine-tuned LoRAs.
Multiple steering vectors can be applied simultaneously, showing synergistic effects and functionality fusion.
By scaling the steering vector, varying degrees of behavior intensity can be achieved, allowing for personalized control.
papers.limitation: The steering vector only affects a single layer in the transformer; a multi-layer design might improve results.
future_direction: Exploring multi-layer steering designs for potentially better results.
papers.abstract: Researchers have been studying approaches to steer the behavior of Large Language Models (LLMs) and build personalized LLMs tailored for various applications. While fine-tuning seems to be a direct solution, it requires substantial computational resources and may significantly affect the utility of the original LLM. Recent endeavors have introduced more lightweight strategies, focusing on extracting "steering vectors" to guide the model's output toward desired behaviors by adjusting activations within specific layers of the LLM's transformer architecture. However, such steering vectors are directly extracted from the activations of human preference data and thus often lead to suboptimal results and occasional failures, especially in alignment-related scenarios. This work proposes an innovative approach that could produce more effective steering vectors through bi-directional preference optimization. Our method is designed to allow steering vectors to directly influence the generation probability of contrastive human preference data pairs, thereby offering a more precise representation of the target behavior. By carefully adjusting the direction and magnitude of the steering vector, we enabled personalized control over the desired behavior across a spectrum of intensities. Extensive experimentation across various open-ended generation tasks, particularly focusing on steering AI personas, has validated the efficacy of our approach. Moreover, we comprehensively investigate critical alignment-concerning scenarios, such as managing truthfulness, mitigating hallucination, and addressing jailbreaking attacks. Remarkably, our method can still demonstrate outstanding steering effectiveness across these scenarios. Furthermore, we showcase the transferability of our steering vectors across different models/LoRAs and highlight the synergistic benefits of applying multiple vectors simultaneously.

papers.title: Locating and Mitigating Gender Bias in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the locations and generation mechanisms of gender bias in large language models, and how can it be mitigated effectively while preserving model capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: This paper integrates locating and mitigating gender bias in a unified framework, using causal mediation analysis to trace bias to bottom MLP and top attention modules, and proposes the LSDM knowledge-editing method to effectively debias while preserving model capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Gender bias in LLMs is generated by the bottom MLP modules and extracted by top attention modules; the LSDM method effectively mitigates this bias while preserving model capabilities and can be extended to unseen occupational pronouns.
papers.key_findings:
The bottom MLP modules acting on the last token of occupational pronouns and the top attention modules acting on the final word are primary contributors to gender bias generation.
The proposed LSDM method reduces gender bias by an average of 71.4% across tested models and datasets.
LSDM outperforms fine-tuning and counterfactual data augmentation baselines in debiasing effectiveness and in preserving model performance on knowledge and reasoning tasks.
LSDM mitigates catastrophic forgetting, maintaining model capabilities on seven proficiency test datasets.
LSDM can generalize to reduce bias in some unseen neutral occupational pronouns, though effectiveness is reduced for out-of-distribution cases.
papers.limitation:
The collective influence of model components on the output has not been extensively studied.
LSDM's effectiveness remains poor for occupational pronouns outside the distribution.
The method focuses only on gender bias in occupational pronouns; extending to a broader range of biases is future work.
future_direction: Delve deeper into the mechanics of the debias method to thoroughly understand and apply it to enhance the model's knowledge performance.
Extend the method to a broader range of biases beyond gender and occupational pronouns.
papers.abstract: Large language models(LLM) are pre-trained on extensive corpora to learn facts and human cognition which contain human preferences. However, this process can inadvertently lead to these models acquiring biases and stereotypes prevalent in society. Prior research has typically tackled the issue of bias through a one-dimensional perspective, concentrating either on locating or mitigating it. This limited perspective has created obstacles in facilitating research on bias to synergistically complement and progressively build upon one another. In this study, we integrate the processes of locating and mitigating bias within a unified framework. Initially, we use causal mediation analysis to trace the causal effects of different components' activation within a large language model. Building on this, we propose the LSDM (Least Square Debias Method), a knowledge-editing based method for mitigating gender bias in occupational pronouns, and compare it against two baselines on three gender bias datasets and seven knowledge competency test datasets. The experimental results indicate that the primary contributors to gender bias are the bottom MLP modules acting on the last token of occupational pronouns and the top attention module acting on the final word in the sentence. Furthermore, LSDM mitigates gender bias in the model more effectively than the other baselines, while fully preserving the model's capabilities in all other aspects.

papers.title: The LLM Language Network: A Neuroscientific Approach for Identifying Causally Task-Relevant Units
papers.research_question: Does specialization for language (and other cognitive domains) emerge in large language models, and what is the causal role of such specialized units?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired method to identify language-selective units in LLMs and demonstrates their causal role in language processing through ablation studies.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop specialized language units that are causally important for language processing, similar to the human brain, but specialization for other cognitive domains is less consistent.
papers.key_findings:
Language-selective units can be identified in LLMs using the same functional localization method as in neuroscience.
Ablating even a small percentage (e.g., 1%) of language-selective units causes significant performance drops in language tasks, while ablating random units does not.
The language-selective units in LLMs show similar response profiles to the human language network (e.g., stronger responses to sentences than to non-words, arithmetic, or code).
The language-selective units are more aligned to brain recordings from the human language network than random units, especially when selecting a small subset of units.
Specialization for other cognitive domains (reasoning and theory of mind) is not consistently found across LLMs, with only a subset of models showing such specialization.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focused on models smaller than 13 billion parameters, which may not capture specialization in larger models.
They evaluated Theory of Mind and Multiple Demand units using only one benchmark each (TOMi for ToM and MATH for MD), which may not be comprehensive.
The localizers are adapted from neuroscience and may be constrained by the stimuli sets traditionally used in neuroscience.
future_direction: Expanding the study to include more models and a broader set of benchmarks.
Developing more targeted and robust localizers not restricted by neuroscience stimuli.
Analyzing varying numbers of selective units for MD and ToM networks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities on not just language tasks, but also various tasks that are not linguistic in nature, such as logical reasoning and social inference. In the human brain, neuroscience has identified a core language system that selectively and causally supports language processing. We here ask whether similar specialization for language emerges in LLMs. We identify language-selective units within 18 popular LLMs, using the same localization approach that is used in neuroscience. We then establish the causal role of these units by demonstrating that ablating LLM language-selective units -- but not random units -- leads to drastic deficits in language tasks. Correspondingly, language-selective LLM units are more aligned to brain recordings from the human language system than random units. Finally, we investigate whether our localization method extends to other cognitive domains: while we find specialized networks in some LLMs for reasoning and social capabilities, there are substantial differences among models. These findings provide functional and causal evidence for specialization in large language models, and highlight parallels with the functional organization in the brain.

papers.title: Brittle Minds, Fixable Activations: Understanding Belief Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal belief representations emerge in language models? Are they structured or spurious? How robust are they to prompt variations? Can they be strengthened?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that belief representations in language models improve with model size and fine-tuning, are structured yet brittle to prompt variations, and can be strengthened using contrastive activation addition to correct wrong Theory of Mind inferences.
papers.conclusion: Belief representations in language models are structured but brittle, and they can be strengthened via activation editing, offering a path toward more reliable Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Belief representations emerge in consistent patterns across models, improve with model size, and benefit significantly from fine-tuning, especially in smaller models.
Control tasks and PCA show that belief representations are structured and not spurious.
Representations of others' beliefs are brittle to semantically neutral prompt variations.
Contrastive activation addition (CAA) can strengthen belief representations and improve ToM performance across different tasks.
CAA steering vectors are general and transferable to other ToM tasks, yielding substantial performance gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focused on one dataset (BigToM) and a limited set of model families due to computational constraints.
The approach could be extended to other mental states beyond beliefs.
future_direction: Exploring how different types of fine-tuning influence the emergence of internal belief representations.
Developing robustness benchmarks and new approaches to improve generalization of belief representations.
Directly embedding perspective-taking circuits into model architectures.
papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in Theory of Mind (ToM) tasks for evaluating language models (LMs), little is known about how LMs internally represent mental states of self and others. Understanding these internal mechanisms is critical - not only to move beyond surface-level performance, but also for model alignment and safety, where subtle misattributions of mental states may go undetected in generated outputs. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of belief representations in LMs by probing models across different scales, training regimens, and prompts - using control tasks to rule out confounds. Our experiments provide evidence that both model size and fine-tuning substantially improve LMs' internal representations of others' beliefs, which are structured - not mere by-products of spurious correlations - yet brittle to prompt variations. Crucially, we show that these representations can be strengthened: targeted edits to model activations can correct wrong ToM inferences.

papers.title: Interpreting Bias in Large Language Models: A Feature-Based Approach
papers.research_question: How do biases propagate in large language models, and how can they be interpreted and mitigated using a feature-based approach?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a feature-based method for analyzing and mitigating gender bias in LLMs, identifying the roles of MLPs and attention heads in bias propagation, and demonstrating targeted debiasing using counterfactual datasets.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a novel feature-based approach for interpreting and mitigating gender bias in LLMs, showing that targeted interventions can reduce bias and providing insights into bias mechanisms for future ethical AI development.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias in LLMs originates in early layers, primarily through MLPs, as shown by activation patching experiments.
Attention heads copy bias from profession tokens to final token positions, propagating bias through the network, validated via attribution patching.
Targeted debiasing by fine-tuning identified components (MLPs or attention heads) can reduce bias, but effectiveness varies across models and may be limited by dataset size.
The feature-based approach is extensible to other forms of gender bias, such as stereotypes in household duties, by mapping features to model components.
Patching MLP outputs or attention heads can reverse biased logit orders without losing profession information in generated text, indicating selective intervention.
papers.limitation:
Potential compensation phenomenon where other components take over after patching, which may affect analysis.
Restricted to English language bias only, limiting generalizability.
The approach may require case-by-case tweaking, which is not scalable for multiple biases.
future_direction: Exploring bias interactions in multilingual settings
Examining the impact of debiasing across languages from a white-box perspective
Investigating applicability to other areas like AI security and alignment
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) such as Mistral and LLaMA have showcased remarkable performance across various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. Despite their success, these models inherit social biases from the diverse datasets on which they are trained. This paper investigates the propagation of biases within LLMs through a novel feature-based analytical approach. Drawing inspiration from causal mediation analysis, we hypothesize the evolution of bias-related features and validate them using interpretability techniques like activation and attribution patching. Our contributions are threefold: (1) We introduce and empirically validate a feature-based method for bias analysis in LLMs, applied to LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-3-8B, and Mistral-7B-v0.3 with templates from a professions dataset. (2) We extend our method to another form of gender bias, demonstrating its generalizability. (3) We differentiate the roles of MLPs and attention heads in bias propagation and implement targeted debiasing using a counterfactual dataset. Our findings reveal the complex nature of bias in LLMs and emphasize the necessity for tailored debiasing strategies, offering a deeper understanding of bias mechanisms and pathways for effective mitigation.

papers.title: Truth-value judgment in language models:belief directions are context sensitive
papers.research_question: How does context impact the behavior of belief probes (directions predictive of truth) in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates the context sensitivity and consistency of belief probes across layers and models, shows belief directions are causal mediators in natural language inference, and introduces a more stable variant of Contrast Consistent Search (CCR).
papers.conclusion: The results suggest that belief directions are causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.
papers.key_findings:
Belief probes are generally context sensitive but are also sensitive to irrelevant contexts and can update probabilities incorrectly.
The type of errors made by probes depend on the layer, the model type, and the kind of data.
Belief directions are (one of the) causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.
Instruction-tuning makes models more likely to represent prior assertions as true, even if they conflict with the model's own evaluation.
papers.limitation: The difficulty of separating hypothetical LLM 'beliefs' from commonly-held beliefs, as probes might identify features correlated with truth in the training data rather than an objective evaluation of truth.
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that the latent spaces of large language models (LLMs) contain directions predictive of the truth of sentences. Multiple methods recover such directions and build probes that are described as getting at a model's "knowledge" or "beliefs". We investigate this phenomenon, looking closely at the impact of context on the probes. Our experiments establish where in the LLM the probe's predictions can be described as being conditional on the preceding (related) sentences. Specifically, we quantify the responsiveness of the probes to the presence of (negated) supporting and contradicting sentences, and score the probes on their consistency. We also perform a causal intervention experiment, investigating whether moving the representation of a premise along these belief directions influences the position of the hypothesis along that same direction. We find that the probes we test are generally context sensitive, but that contexts which should not affect the truth often still impact the probe outputs. Our experiments show that the type of errors depend on the layer, the (type of) model, and the kind of data. Finally, our results suggest that belief directions are (one of the) causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.

papers.title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms of refusal behavior in language models? Specifically, is refusal mediated by a single direction in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: Refusal in language models is mediated by a single direction in the residual stream; this direction can be extracted via difference-in-means and used to control refusal behavior through weight orthogonalization, enabling a white-box jailbreak.
papers.conclusion: Current safety fine-tuning methods are brittle, and understanding model internals can lead to practical methods for controlling model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace across 13 open-source chat models up to 72B parameters.
Ablating this 'refusal direction' from the residual stream prevents the model from refusing harmful instructions.
Adding this direction to activations induces refusal on even harmless instructions.
Weight orthogonalization, a novel white-box jailbreak method that modifies model weights to erase the refusal direction, effectively disables refusal with minimal impact on other capabilities.
Adversarial suffixes suppress the refusal direction by hijacking the attention of important heads away from the harmful instruction.
papers.limitation:
The string-matching approach for refusal score is effective at detecting memorized refusals but does not assess coherence or harmfulness of completions.
The weight orthogonalization jailbreak is less effective when the model's default system prompt is included, indicating system prompt sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Conversational large language models are fine-tuned for both instruction-following and safety, resulting in models that obey benign requests but refuse harmful ones. While this refusal behavior is widespread across chat models, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we show that refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, across 13 popular open-source chat models up to 72B parameters in size. Specifically, for each model, we find a single direction such that erasing this direction from the model's residual stream activations prevents it from refusing harmful instructions, while adding this direction elicits refusal on even harmless instructions. Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel white-box jailbreak method that surgically disables refusal with minimal effect on other capabilities. Finally, we mechanistically analyze how adversarial suffixes suppress propagation of the refusal-mediating direction. Our findings underscore the brittleness of current safety fine-tuning methods. More broadly, our work showcases how an understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical methods for controlling model behavior.

papers.title: Extending Activation Steering to Broad Skills and Multiple Behaviours
papers.research_question: Can we extend activation steering to broad skills and multiple behaviours?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering can be applied to broad skills (coding) with similar effectiveness as narrow skills, and simultaneous injection of multiple steering vectors at different layers is more promising than combining them into a single vector.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering can be extended to broad skills and multiple behaviours, with simultaneous steering being a promising direction.
papers.key_findings:
Steering to reduce general coding ability is competitive with steering to reduce Python-specific ability.
Individual steering vectors for behaviours like myopia and wealth-seeking are effective.
Combining multiple steering vectors into one vector is largely unsuccessful.
Simultaneous injection of individual steering vectors at different layers is promising and has minor alignment tax.
Steering at layer 0 for coding ability had an opposite effect, possibly due to copy suppression.
papers.limitation:
The flexibility of activation steering makes finding optimal setups non-trivial.
It is unclear whether reductions in matching scores (e.g., a 20% reduction in coding accuracy) translate to real-world risk reduction.
future_direction: Testing with other models to understand the general working of activation steering.
Using different injection coefficients for different steering vectors in simultaneous steering.
Generating and injecting steering vectors at different places within a layer (e.g., attention and MLP components).
Steering against alternative programming languages to further investigate broad steering.
papers.abstract: Current large language models have dangerous capabilities, which are likely to become more problematic in the future. Activation steering techniques can be used to reduce risks from these capabilities. In this paper, we investigate the efficacy of activation steering for broad skills and multiple behaviours. First, by comparing the effects of reducing performance on general coding ability and Python-specific ability, we find that steering broader skills is competitive to steering narrower skills. Second, we steer models to become more or less myopic and wealth-seeking, among other behaviours. In our experiments, combining steering vectors for multiple different behaviours into one steering vector is largely unsuccessful. On the other hand, injecting individual steering vectors at different places in a model simultaneously is promising.

papers.title: Identifying and Manipulating Personality Traits in LLMs Through Activation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can personality traits in large language models be identified and manipulated using activation engineering to enable dynamic personality adjustment without extensive retraining?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces 'feature induction', a method for identifying and manipulating personality traits in LLMs through activation engineering, enabling dynamic personality customization without extensive retraining.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that activation engineering can be used to identify and manipulate personality traits in LLMs, enabling dynamic customization without retraining, while highlighting ethical implications.
papers.key_findings:
Layer 18 in Llama 3 8B is the most influential layer for personality trait expression.
Personality traits can be clustered into meaningful groups based on activation vectors, revealing semantic relationships.
Principal component analysis identifies key personality dimensions and traits that capture most variance.
Socially undesirable personality traits are grouped together in activation space, with proximal traits like competitive and confident.
An interactive interface allows real-time control of LLM personality by adjusting principal component weights.
future_direction: Enhancing interpretability by mapping personality traits to specific layer activations and neurons.
Analyzing the performance consequences of different personality factors on LLM competencies.
Extending the research to multilingual models to understand cultural specificity of personality traits.
papers.abstract: The field of large language models (LLMs) has grown rapidly in recent years, driven by the desire for better efficiency, interpretability, and safe use. Building on the novel approach of "activation engineering," this study explores personality modification in LLMs, drawing inspiration from research like Refusal in LLMs Is Mediated by a Single Direction (arXiv:2406.11717) and Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition (arXiv:2312.06681). We leverage activation engineering to develop a method for identifying and adjusting activation directions related to personality traits, which may allow for dynamic LLM personality fine-tuning. This work aims to further our understanding of LLM interpretability while examining the ethical implications of such developments.

papers.title: Exploring the Personality Traits of LLMs through Latent Features Steering
papers.research_question: How do long-term background factors and short-term pressures shape and influence the personality traits of LLMs? How can these factors influence LLMs’ safety?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training-free method to extract and steer latent features in LLMs to control personality traits, and analyzes the impact of these traits on model safety.
papers.conclusion: The study's method allows for understanding and controlling personality traits in LLMs, which is important for developing personalized AI systems aligned with human values.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models (9B) show more stable personality traits under feature steering compared to smaller models (2B).
Extracted features effectively steer model behavior in social bias tasks, as shown by increased logit differences.
Personality traits can be manipulated by steering long-term background and short-term pressure features.
Safety is affected by personality traits; for example, offensive content is highly sensitive to changes in background features.
The method enables fine-grained control of personality without retraining.
papers.limitation: Training SAEs for LLMs requires substantial computational resources, so the experiments were limited to using pre-trained SAE models, which may limit generalizability to larger-scale models.
future_direction: Explore more efficient methods for extracting precise internal features and enabling fine-grained control of model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have significantly advanced dialogue systems and role-playing agents through their ability to generate human-like text. While prior studies have shown that LLMs can exhibit distinct and consistent personalities, the mechanisms through which these models encode and express specific personality traits remain poorly understood. To address this, we investigate how various factors, such as cultural norms and environmental stressors, encoded within LLMs, shape their personality traits, guided by the theoretical framework of social determinism. Inspired by related work on LLM interpretability, we propose a training-free approach to modify the model's behavior by extracting and steering latent features corresponding to factors within the model, thereby eliminating the need for retraining. Furthermore, we analyze the implications of these factors for model safety, focusing on their impact through the lens of personality.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: Towards Unifying Interpretability and Control: Evaluation via Intervention
papers.research_question: How well can interpretability methods control model behavior through interventions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a unifying framework and two evaluation metrics (intervention success rate and coherence-intervention tradeoff) to assess interpretability methods' ability to control model behavior, finding that current methods are inconsistent and often compromise coherence.
papers.conclusion: Current interpretability methods have limitations in achieving control without degrading output quality, and lens-based methods are more effective for simple interventions.
papers.key_findings:
While current interpretability methods allow for intervention, their effectiveness is inconsistent across features and models.
Lens-based methods (Logit Lens and Tuned Lens) outperform SAEs and probes in achieving simple, concrete interventions.
Mechanistic interventions often compromise model coherence, underperforming simpler alternatives like prompting.
Sparse autoencoders have high error rates in feature labeling, leading to lower intervention success.
Probes and steering vectors learn spurious correlations, affecting their intervention performance.
papers.limitation: Interventions often compromise model coherence, leading to repetitive or incoherent outputs.
papers.abstract: With the growing complexity and capability of large language models, a need to understand model reasoning has emerged, often motivated by an underlying goal of controlling and aligning models. While numerous interpretability and steering methods have been proposed as solutions, they are typically designed either for understanding or for control, seldom addressing both. Additionally, the lack of standardized applications, motivations, and evaluation metrics makes it difficult to assess methods' practical utility and efficacy. To address the aforementioned issues, we argue that intervention is a fundamental goal of interpretability and introduce success criteria to evaluate how well methods can control model behavior through interventions. To evaluate existing methods for this ability, we unify and extend four popular interpretability methods-sparse autoencoders, logit lens, tuned lens, and probing-into an abstract encoder-decoder framework, enabling interventions on interpretable features that can be mapped back to latent representations to control model outputs. We introduce two new evaluation metrics: intervention success rate and coherence-intervention tradeoff, designed to measure the accuracy of explanations and their utility in controlling model behavior. Our findings reveal that (1) while current methods allow for intervention, their effectiveness is inconsistent across features and models, (2) lens-based methods outperform SAEs and probes in achieving simple, concrete interventions, and (3) mechanistic interventions often compromise model coherence, underperforming simpler alternatives, such as prompting, and highlighting a critical shortcoming of current interpretability approaches in applications requiring control.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language when processing non-English prompts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that multilingual language models like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate representations favoring English before shifting to the target language.
papers.conclusion: The evidence suggests that the abstract 'concept space' in multilingual transformers lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding linguistic biases.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate embeddings in middle layers decode to English versions of the correct next token, even when the input and output are non-English.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space (high entropy, no language), concept space (low entropy, English dominates), and output space (target language dominates).
The concept space is biased towards English, indicating an internal pivot language.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The token energy metric shows that latent embeddings have low energy in middle layers and high energy in later layers when the target language is selected.
papers.limitation:
Focus on the Llama-2 family limits generalizability to other models.
Tasks are simple and provide a highly controlled, toy-like context.
Limited understanding of the structure of the concept space in its original high-dimensional form.
The logit lens only grants approximate access to internal beliefs about output; other information remains hidden.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias changes when decreasing the dominance of English during training, e.g., by using different language mixtures or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks, including more culturally sensitive problems and popular use-cases.
Better understand and map out the concept space in its high-dimensional form.
papers.abstract: We ask whether multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language -- a question of key importance for understanding how language models function and the origins of linguistic bias. Focusing on the Llama-2 family of transformer models, our study uses carefully constructed non-English prompts with a unique correct single-token continuation. From layer to layer, transformers gradually map an input embedding of the final prompt token to an output embedding from which next-token probabilities are computed. Tracking intermediate embeddings through their high-dimensional space reveals three distinct phases, whereby intermediate embeddings (1) start far away from output token embeddings; (2) already allow for decoding a semantically correct next token in the middle layers, but give higher probability to its version in English than in the input language; (3) finally move into an input-language-specific region of the embedding space. We cast these results into a conceptual model where the three phases operate in "input space", "concept space", and "output space", respectively. Crucially, our evidence suggests that the abstract "concept space" lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding the biases held by multilingual language models.

papers.title: Enhancing Multiple Dimensions of Trustworthiness in LLMs via Sparse Activation Control
papers.research_question: How can we enhance multiple dimensions of trustworthiness (safety, factuality, bias) in LLMs simultaneously without training, by controlling sparse activations in specific model components?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Activation Control, a training-free method that enhances multiple trustworthiness dimensions in LLMs by identifying sparse, task-specific attention heads and controlling their representations using Gaussian Mixture Models, avoiding control conflicts.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Activation Control is an effective training-free method for enhancing multi-dimensional trustworthiness in LLMs by leveraging sparse and independent task-specific components.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse Activation Control can enhance safety, factuality, and bias simultaneously without significant interference, outperforming representation engineering baselines in multi-task control.
Attention heads for different tasks are sparse and have minimal overlap, allowing independent control.
The method does not significantly harm general model performance on MMLU and CSQA.
The method generalizes to other models (Qwen series) and additional trustworthiness tasks (robustness, privacy).
Control shifts head outputs towards task-relevant tokens, as shown by unembedding projections.
papers.limitation:
Relies on construction of paired stimuli, which may require domain knowledge.
Experiments are limited to a few models and tasks.
future_direction: Extend to more tasks and models
Explore theoretical foundations of sparsity
papers.abstract: As the development and application of Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance rapidly, enhancing their trustworthiness and aligning them with human preferences has become a critical area of research. Traditional methods rely heavily on extensive data for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), but representation engineering offers a new, training-free approach. This technique leverages semantic features to control the representation of LLM's intermediate hidden states, enabling the model to meet specific requirements such as increased honesty or heightened safety awareness. However, a significant challenge arises when attempting to fulfill multiple requirements simultaneously. It proves difficult to encode various semantic contents, like honesty and safety, into a singular semantic feature, restricting its practicality. In this work, we address this issue through ``Sparse Activation Control''. By delving into the intrinsic mechanisms of LLMs, we manage to identify and pinpoint components that are closely related to specific tasks within the model, i.e., attention heads. These heads display sparse characteristics that allow for near-independent control over different tasks. Our experiments, conducted on the open-source Llama series models, have yielded encouraging results. The models were able to align with human preferences on issues of safety, factuality, and bias concurrently.

papers.title: Does Transformer Interpretability Transfer to RNNs?
papers.research_question: Does transformer interpretability transfer to RNNs? Specifically, do contrastive activation addition, the tuned lens, and methods for eliciting latent knowledge work on RNNs like Mamba and RWKV?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that popular transformer interpretability methods (contrastive activation addition, the tuned lens, and methods for eliciting latent knowledge) transfer to state-of-the-art RNN architectures, and that the compressed state of RNNs can be used to enhance activation addition for steering.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability tools designed for transformers largely work out-of-the-box for RNNs, with similar performance, and the compressed state of RNNs can be used to enhance activation addition for steering.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive activation addition (CAA) is effective for steering RNNs, with middle layers showing the greatest effect.
State steering, using the internal state of RNNs, is possible and can be combined with activation steering, though the effects are not additive.
The tuned lens can be applied to RNNs, with perplexity decreasing monotonically with depth, similar to transformers.
Linear probes trained on 'Alice' contexts can predict the correct answer in 'Bob' contexts for RNNs, similar to transformers.
papers.limitation: The work did not explore mechanistic or circuit-based interpretability tools, focusing instead on representation-based methods.
future_direction: Further exploration of the RNN state for extracting latent knowledge or predictions.
Examination of the applicability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to RNNs.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in recurrent neural network architectures, such as Mamba and RWKV, have enabled RNNs to match or exceed the performance of equal-size transformers in terms of language modeling perplexity and downstream evaluations, suggesting that future systems may be built on completely new architectures. In this paper, we examine if selected interpretability methods originally designed for transformer language models will transfer to these up-and-coming recurrent architectures. Specifically, we focus on steering model outputs via contrastive activation addition, on eliciting latent predictions via the tuned lens, and eliciting latent knowledge from models fine-tuned to produce false outputs under certain conditions. Our results show that most of these techniques are effective when applied to RNNs, and we show that it is possible to improve some of them by taking advantage of RNNs' compressed state.

papers.title: Extending Token Computation for LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What is the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance? Can extending the Chain-of-Thought chain within the same prompt improve reasoning outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel algorithm that extends computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought process by optimizing attention mechanisms, which improves reasoning capabilities, especially in non-STEM domains.
papers.conclusion: The study introduces an attention optimization method that enhances LLM reasoning, particularly in non-STEM domains, and sets the groundwork for more transparent and adaptable models for real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing the number of computed tokens enhances LLM reasoning performance.
Attention patterns in middle layers are skewed by non-semantic tokens with high attention scores, which hinders reasoning.
The proposed algorithm re-balances attention distributions by emulating early layer attention patterns, leading to more extended and logical reasoning steps.
The method improves reasoning in non-STEM domains but may reduce accuracy in memory-dependent questions due to error propagation.
Larger models (e.g., 13B) show greater improvement with the method compared to smaller models (e.g., 7B).
papers.limitation:
The method reduces accuracy by 3 percentage points in memory-dependent questions from the MMLU dataset.
Extended reasoning may amplify error propagation in STEM categories where the model's reasoning capabilities are not robust.
Scarcity of logical process examples for STEM questions in training data may hinder performance.
future_direction: Integrate a training phase to enhance memory recall for early-answering questions.
Reduce memory and computational demands using techniques like ghost attention mechanisms.
Enhance interpretability of attention patterns across layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are pivotal in advancing natural language processing but often struggle with complex reasoning tasks due to inefficient attention distributions. In this paper, we explore the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance and introduce a novel method for extending computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process, utilizing attention mechanism optimization. By fine-tuning an LLM on a domain-specific, highly structured dataset, we analyze attention patterns across layers, identifying inefficiencies caused by non-semantic tokens with outlier high attention scores. To address this, we propose an algorithm that emulates early layer attention patterns across downstream layers to re-balance skewed attention distributions and enhance knowledge abstraction. Our findings demonstrate that our approach not only facilitates a deeper understanding of the internal dynamics of LLMs but also significantly improves their reasoning capabilities, particularly in non-STEM domains. Our study lays the groundwork for further innovations in LLM design, aiming to create more powerful, versatile, and responsible models capable of tackling a broad range of real-world applications.

papers.title: Truth-value judgment in language models: 'truth directions' are context sensitive
papers.research_question: How does context affect the truth-value probes in large language models, and are these probes coherently incorporating contextual information?
papers.core_contribution: Truth-value probes are context sensitive but also sensitive to irrelevant information, and truth-value directions causally mediate natural language inference.
papers.conclusion: Truth-value directions are context sensitive and causally mediate inference, but probes are not fully coherent.
papers.key_findings:
Truth-value probes are sensitive to context, but also to irrelevant information.
The type of errors (consistency errors) depend on the layer, model, and data.
Probes trained without premises (no-prem) still show context sensitivity, indicating that prior beliefs are not represented independently.
Instruction-tuned models show different error patterns (more E4 errors) compared to pretrained-only models.
Truth-value directions causally mediate natural language inference (intervention experiment).
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that the latent spaces of large language models (LLMs) contain directions predictive of the truth of sentences. Multiple methods recover such directions and build probes that are described as uncovering a model's "knowledge" or "beliefs". We investigate this phenomenon, looking closely at the impact of context on the probes. Our experiments establish where in the LLM the probe's predictions are (most) sensitive to the presence of related sentences, and how to best characterize this kind of sensitivity. We do so by measuring different types of consistency errors that occur after probing an LLM whose inputs consist of hypotheses preceded by (negated) supporting and contradicting sentences. We also perform a causal intervention experiment, investigating whether moving the representation of a premise along these truth-value directions influences the position of an entailed or contradicted sentence along that same direction. We find that the probes we test are generally context sensitive, but that contexts which should not affect the truth often still impact the probe outputs. Our experiments show that the type of errors depend on the layer, the model, and the kind of data. Finally, our results suggest that truth-value directions are causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.

papers.title: Analysing the Generalisation and Reliability ofSteering Vectors
papers.research_question: What are the reliability and generalisation properties of steering vectors for adjusting language model behaviour at inference time?
papers.core_contribution: This work rigorously investigates the reliability and generalization of steering vectors, showing they have substantial limitations both in- and out-of-distribution, including high variance in steerability across inputs and brittleness to prompt changes.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors in their current form are not a panacea for aligning model behavior at inference time; more work is required to ensure they reliably produce desired behavior in a generalisable way.
papers.key_findings:
In-distribution steerability is highly variable across inputs, with many examples being anti-steerable (steered in the opposite direction).
Steerability is affected by spurious factors like token and position bias, which are not fixable by simple dataset debiasing.
Out-of-distribution, steering vectors often generalize reasonably well but are brittle to reasonable changes in the prompt.
Steerability is mostly a property of the dataset used for extraction rather than the model architecture.
Similarity in the unsteered model behavior between source and target prompt settings is correlated with steering vector generalization.
papers.limitation:
The study uses a large number of datasets, but even more variety in the type of behavior being steered towards could be studied to ensure robustness.
The failures of steering vectors are not entirely understood, and it is unclear what potential mitigations could be applied.
Only two models are analyzed in this work, although they use different sizes, architectures, training data and algorithms.
future_direction: Investigating what causes steerability biases and whether other techniques for extracting and applying SVs can mitigate these biases.
Investigating methods to improve SV generalisation, and investigating scenarios where they generalise better or worse.
Developing methods to disentangle separate sub-behaviours in an unsupervised way for unsteerable behaviours.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors (SVs) are a new approach to efficiently adjust language model behaviour at inference time by intervening on intermediate model activations. They have shown promise in terms of improving both capabilities and model alignment. However, the reliability and generalisation properties of this approach are unknown. In this work, we rigorously investigate these properties, and show that steering vectors have substantial limitations both in- and out-of-distribution. In-distribution, steerability is highly variable across different inputs. Depending on the concept, spurious biases can substantially contribute to how effective steering is for each input, presenting a challenge for the widespread use of steering vectors. Out-of-distribution, while steering vectors often generalise well, for several concepts they are brittle to reasonable changes in the prompt, resulting in them failing to generalise well. Overall, our findings show that while steering can work well in the right circumstances, there remain many technical difficulties of applying steering vectors to guide models' behaviour at scale.

papers.title: Personality Alignment of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can large language models be aligned with the unique personality traits and preferences of individual users, as opposed to general human values?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel personality alignment framework comprising the PAPI dataset for evaluating alignment across positive and negative personality dimensions and the PAS method, which efficiently aligns LLMs to individual preferences via activation interventions without weight updates.
papers.conclusion: Personality alignment is a crucial step towards human-centered AI, and the proposed PAS method provides an efficient, training-free approach to tailor LLM behavior to individual user preferences, paving the way for more meaningful AI interactions.
papers.key_findings:
The PAS method achieves superior personality alignment performance compared to DPO and PPO, requiring only 1/5 of the optimization time.
PAS applied to Llama-3-8B-Instruct can outperform the GPT-4o model on personality alignment tasks.
The PAPI dataset, with over 320,000 samples from multiple personality inventories, enables comprehensive evaluation of LLM alignment across both adaptive and maladaptive personality traits.
Activation interventions for personality alignment are highly parameter-efficient, storing only about 1/10,000,000 of the parameters compared to a full-parameter model.
The method demonstrates generalization capabilities in open-ended generation and complex reasoning tasks while maintaining aligned personality traits.
papers.abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) typically aim to reflect general human values and behaviors, but they often fail to capture the unique characteristics and preferences of individual users. To address this gap, we introduce the concept of Personality Alignment. This approach tailors LLMs' responses and decisions to match the specific preferences of individual users or closely related groups. Inspired by psychometrics, we created the Personality Alignment with Personality Inventories (PAPI) dataset, which includes data from over 320,000 real subjects across multiple personality assessments, including both the Big Five Personality Factors and Dark Triad traits. This comprehensive dataset enables quantitative evaluation of LLMs' alignment capabilities across both positive and potentially problematic personality dimensions. Recognizing the challenges of personality alignments, such as limited personal data, diverse preferences, and scalability requirements, we developed an activation intervention optimization method. This method enhances LLMs' ability to efficiently align with individual behavioral preferences using minimal data and computational resources. Remarkably, our method, PAS, achieves superior performance while requiring only 1/5 of the optimization time compared to DPO, offering practical value for personality alignment. Our work paves the way for future AI systems to make decisions and reason in truly personality ways, enhancing the relevance and meaning of AI interactions for each user and advancing human-centered artificial intelligence. The dataset and code are released at https://github.com/zhu-minjun/PAlign.

papers.title: Improving Steering Vectors by Targeting Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we improve steering vectors to target specific SAE features and achieve desired model behaviors while minimizing unintended side effects?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to measure steering effects using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and uses this to develop SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which constructs steering vectors to target specific SAE features while minimizing unintended side effects.
papers.conclusion: SAE-TS is an effective method for steering language models, balancing desired behavioral changes with output coherence better than existing baselines.
papers.key_findings:
Developed a method to quantify and interpret the effects of steering interventions on SAE features.
Introduced SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which learns a linear relationship between steering vectors and their effects on SAE features to construct targeted steering vectors.
SAE-TS outperforms existing methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and direct SAE feature steering on most tasks, achieving better alignment with intended behavior while maintaining coherence.
The method allows for more predictable and controllable steering of language models compared to prior approaches.
Provides an interactive tool (EffectVis) for exploring feature effects and relationships.
papers.limitation:
Investigations were limited to Gemma-2 2B and 9B models, which share the same distilled architecture, so results may not transfer to other models.
Focused on base models without instruction tuning, so the study did not investigate tasks and features relevant for safety or capabilities.
Steering is limited to concepts present in the SAE, which may not cover all concepts due to feature splitting or niche features only appearing in very large SAEs.
future_direction: Apply steering methods to chat models and safety-relevant steering targets.
Explore different SAE architectures (e.g., TopK SAEs) and test on various model architectures beyond the Gemma family.
Adapt BiPO to optimize steering vectors towards desired feature effects.
papers.abstract: To control the behavior of language models, steering methods attempt to ensure that outputs of the model satisfy specific pre-defined properties. Adding steering vectors to the model is a promising method of model control that is easier than finetuning, and may be more robust than prompting. However, it can be difficult to anticipate the effects of steering vectors produced by methods such as CAA [Panickssery et al., 2024] or the direct use of SAE latents [Templeton et al., 2024]. In our work, we address this issue by using SAEs to measure the effects of steering vectors, giving us a method that can be used to understand the causal effect of any steering vector intervention. We use this method for measuring causal effects to develop an improved steering method, SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which finds steering vectors to target specific SAE features while minimizing unintended side effects. We show that overall, SAE-TS balances steering effects with coherence better than CAA and SAE feature steering, when evaluated on a range of tasks.

papers.title: Racing Thoughts: Explaining Contextualization Errors in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What causes contextualization errors in large language models, and can they be explained by race conditions in the model's processing layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the LLM Race Conditions Hypothesis to explain contextualization errors in LLMs, providing correlational and causal evidence through mechanistic interpretability techniques.
papers.conclusion: The LLM Race Conditions Hypothesis explains contextualization errors in LLMs, and inference-time interventions can address them, pointing towards potential architectural solutions.
papers.key_findings:
Injecting distractor text into prompts causes sharp performance degradations in contextualization tasks.
There exists a critical window in middle layers where question tokens integrate information from subject entities.
Model failures are driven by unfinished contextualization of subject entities before this critical window.
Patching interventions such as cross-patching and backpatching can improve performance by addressing race conditions.
Race conditions are endemic to feedforward language models, suggesting architectural limitations.
papers.limitation: Does not comprehensively explain all LLM contextualization errors, such as those due to missing factual knowledge.
future_direction: Explore recurrent connections in models to allow later layer representations to influence earlier ones.
Develop more advanced inference-time interventions based on the findings.
papers.abstract: The profound success of transformer-based language models can largely be attributed to their ability to integrate relevant contextual information from an input sequence in order to generate a response or complete a task. However, we know very little about the algorithms that a model employs to implement this capability, nor do we understand their failure modes. For example, given the prompt "John is going fishing, so he walks over to the bank. Can he make an ATM transaction?", a model may incorrectly respond "Yes" if it has not properly contextualized "bank" as a geographical feature, rather than a financial institution. We propose the LLM Race Conditions Hypothesis as an explanation of contextualization errors of this form. This hypothesis identifies dependencies between tokens (e.g., "bank" must be properly contextualized before the final token, "?", integrates information from "bank"), and claims that contextualization errors are a result of violating these dependencies. Using a variety of techniques from mechanistic intepretability, we provide correlational and causal evidence in support of the hypothesis, and suggest inference-time interventions to address it.

papers.title: A Causal Explainable Guardrails for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we obtain unbiased steering representations in Large Language Models (LLMs) to effectively steer their outputs toward desired attributes while mitigating the confounding effects of semantic biases introduced during pre-training?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes LLMGuardrail, a framework that uses causal analysis and adversarial learning to disentangle and block the confounding effects of semantic biases in LLM representations, enabling the extraction of unbiased steering vectors for controlled text generation.
papers.conclusion: LLMGuardrail effectively addresses the limitations of existing steering methods by incorporating causal analysis to obtain unbiased steering representations, thereby contributing to the development of safer and more reliable LLMs that align with desired attributes.
papers.key_findings:
LLMGuardrail outperforms existing activation engineering baselines (e.g., Activation Addition, Mean-Centring, CCS) in steering LLMs toward desired attributes like truthfulness and away from toxicity, bias, and harmfulness.
The framework's causal debiasing component is crucial for performance, as shown in ablation studies where its removal leads to significant drops in effectiveness.
LLMGuardrail enhances model robustness by reducing the Attack Success Rate (ASR) of various jailbreak attacks, recalibrating attack prompt representations from ambiguous boundary regions back into the unsafe space.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance in natural language tasks, but their outputs can exhibit undesirable attributes or biases.
