papers.conclusion: FairSteer is an effective inference-time debiasing method that mitigates bias in LLMs without requiring retraining, demonstrating broad applicability across tasks while preserving model capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Fairness-related features are linearly separable in the hidden activation space of LLMs, with over 90% linear separability in intermediate layers.
FairSteer effectively reduces bias in question-answering, counterfactual input evaluation, and open-ended text generation tasks across six LLMs.
The method preserves the original model performance on general knowledge tasks (MMLU, ARC, OpenBookQA) and language modeling (WikiText 103).
The Biased Activation Detection (BAD) component is crucial for balancing accuracy and bias reduction; using only the Debiasing Steering Vector (DSV) leads to accuracy drops.
Debiasing Steering Vectors (DSVs) computed from contrast prompt pairs are highly similar across different bias categories, indicating a common underlying structure in the activation space.
papers.limitation:
The reliance on a linear classifier may limit its ability to detect more complex, non-linear forms of bias embedded in model activations.
The effectiveness of the debiasing steering vector depends on the quality and representativeness of the biased-unbiased prompt pairs used during its construction, which may not capture all types of bias present in real-world scenarios.
The approach to derive the debiasing steering vector may not be optimal; the work serves primarily as a proof of concept rather than a thorough exploration of the most effective extraction techniques.
While assessed across six open-source models, the generalizability to other models, especially large-scale proprietary systems and future architectures, remains uncertain.
future_direction: Refine and enhance the methodology for deriving debiasing steering vectors.
Explore adaptive scaling of the intervention strength based on the severity of the bias (using classifier confidence scores).
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are prone to capturing biases from training corpus, leading to potential negative social impacts. Existing prompt-based debiasing methods exhibit instability due to their sensitivity to prompt changes, while fine-tuning-based techniques incur substantial computational overhead and catastrophic forgetting. In this paper, we propose FairSteer, a novel inference-time debiasing framework without requiring customized prompt design or model retraining. Motivated by the linear representation hypothesis, our preliminary investigation demonstrates that fairness-related features can be encoded into separable directions in the hidden activation space. FairSteer operates in three steps: biased activation detection, debiasing steering vector (DSV) computation, and dynamic activation steering. Specifically, it first trains a lightweight linear classifier to detect bias signatures in activations, and then computes DSVs as intervention directions derived from small contrastive prompt pairs. Subsequently, it performs debiasing by adjusting activations with DSVs in the inference stage. Comprehensive evaluation with six LLMs demonstrates the superiority of FairSteer across question-answering, counterfactual input evaluation and open-ended text generation tasks. Code will be released.

papers.title: Activation Steering for Bias Mitigation: An Interpretable Approach to Safer LLMs
papers.research_question: Can bias in large language models be detected and mitigated by probing internal activations and applying steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interpretability-based system that uses linear probes to detect bias in LLM activations and applies steering vectors to mitigate biased outputs in real-time.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that bias can be detected and mitigated through activation steering, offering a transparent method for improving LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on internal activations can detect bias with near-perfect accuracy in later layers of gpt2-large.
Bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers, as shown by increasing probe accuracy.
Steering vectors computed from activation differences can successfully alter biased completions toward more neutral alternatives during inference.
The method provides a direct and interpretable approach to bias mitigation without modifying model weights.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted only on gpt2-large, limiting generalizability to other models.
The training dataset is synthetic, which may not fully represent real-world bias.
future_direction: Investigate whether findings generalize to other model architectures and sizes (e.g., Llama, Mistral).
Validate techniques on real-world datasets of hate speech or bias (e.g., HateXplain, CivilComments).
Explore the use of non-linear probes or more sophisticated steering techniques for more precise control.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more integrated into societal systems, the risk of them perpetuating and amplifying harmful biases becomes a critical safety concern. Traditional methods for mitigating bias often rely on data filtering or post-hoc output moderation, which treat the model as an opaque black box. In this work, we introduce a complete, end-to-end system that uses techniques from mechanistic interpretability to both identify and actively mitigate bias directly within a model's internal workings. Our method involves two primary stages. First, we train linear "probes" on the internal activations of a model to detect the latent representations of various biases (e.g., gender, race, age). Our experiments on \texttt{gpt2-large} demonstrate that these probes can identify biased content with near-perfect accuracy, revealing that bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers. Second, we leverage these findings to compute "steering vectors" by contrasting the model's activation patterns for biased and neutral statements. By adding these vectors during inference, we can actively steer the model's generative process away from producing harmful, stereotypical, or biased content in real-time. We demonstrate the efficacy of this activation steering technique, showing that it successfully alters biased completions toward more neutral alternatives. We present our work as a robust and reproducible system that offers a more direct and interpretable approach to building safer and more accountable LLMs.

papers.title: Steering Risk Preferences in Large Language Models by Aligning Behavioral and Neural Representations
papers.research_question: How can steering vectors be systematically identified to change LLM behavior? The paper proposes a principled approach by aligning latent representations from behavioral methods (Markov chain Monte Carlo with LLMs) with neural counterparts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for deriving steering vectors by aligning behavioral representations (elicited via MCMC with LLMs) with neural activations, enabling precise control of LLM risk preferences without retraining.
papers.conclusion: Self-alignment methods that align behavioral and neural representations offer an effective and principled means of controlling LLM behavior in risk-sensitive contexts.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors derived from aligned behavioral and neural representations (MCMC and Certainty Equivalent methods) outperform Contrastive Activation in steering risky decisions, risk perception, and text generation.
The optimal layer for steering varies: risk perception is more steerable in earlier layers, while risky decisions are more steerable in later layers.
The method allows precise control over risk preferences (risk-seeking vs. risk-averse) across different tasks.
Steering vectors transfer to tasks far from the original elicitation context.
The behavioral representation from MCMC reveals more nuanced risk preferences compared to the Certainty Equivalent method.
papers.limitation:
Further theoretical and mechanistic interpretability research is needed to establish a more concrete link between behaviorally elicited representations and their corresponding neural activations.
Modifying a Transformer’s residual stream is not uniformly effective across all layers; the success of such interventions is highly dependent on the layer selected. Identifying optimal layers for steering remains an open question.
This form of steering is limited in scope for proprietary models where weights are not accessible, restricting its broader applicability.
future_direction: Identifying optimal layers for steering remains an open question for future research.
Future research should consider developing new descriptive frameworks tailored to characterizing and predicting the risky choices of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Changing the behavior of large language models (LLMs) can be as straightforward as editing the Transformer's residual streams using appropriately constructed "steering vectors." These modifications to internal neural activations, a form of representation engineering, offer an effective and targeted means of influencing model behavior without retraining or fine-tuning the model. But how can such steering vectors be systematically identified? We propose a principled approach for uncovering steering vectors by aligning latent representations elicited through behavioral methods (specifically, Markov chain Monte Carlo with LLMs) with their neural counterparts. To evaluate this approach, we focus on extracting latent risk preferences from LLMs and steering their risk-related outputs using the aligned representations as steering vectors. We show that the resulting steering vectors successfully and reliably modulate LLM outputs in line with the targeted behavior.

papers.title: Unsupervised Concept Vector Extraction for Bias Control in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we extract concept representations (like gender) from LLMs without labeled data and use them to measure and manipulate bias?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an unsupervised method (WMD) for extracting concept steering vectors from LLMs and a projection-based intervention method for bias mitigation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method is effective for extracting steering vectors and mitigating bias in LLMs, and it generalizes to other protected attributes like race.
papers.key_findings:
The WMD method extracts steering vectors that have higher correlation with gender bias than the difference-in-means method.
The projection-based intervention effectively reduces gender bias in model predictions.
The method generalizes to racial bias.
Steering vectors can be transferred to different tasks (Winogenerated and occupational stereotypes).
Debiasing via steering does not significantly harm general model capabilities (MMLU and IFEVAL).
papers.limitation:
The approach oversimplifies gender as a binary concept and does not account for non-binary identities.
The method may not be applicable when factual gender information is needed in predictions.
future_direction: Expand evaluation to a broader range of tasks.
Adopt a more comprehensive approach that considers intersectionality of gender with other social identities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are known to perpetuate stereotypes and exhibit biases. Various strategies have been proposed to mitigate these biases, but most work studies biases as a black-box problem without considering how concepts are represented within the model. We adapt techniques from representation engineering to study how the concept of "gender" is represented within LLMs. We introduce a new method that extracts concept representations via probability weighting without labeled data and efficiently selects a steering vector for measuring and manipulating the model's representation. We develop a projection-based method that enables precise steering of model predictions and demonstrate its effectiveness in mitigating gender bias in LLMs and show that it also generalizes to racial bias. Our code is available at: https://github.com/hannahxchen/gender-bias-steering

papers.title: Mechanistic Control of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we control large language models by understanding their inner working mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of language models can be leveraged to control their behavior in various applications, such as reducing hallucination, improving instruction stability, and enhancing planning in dialogues.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation shows that mechanistic control is a promising approach for aligning language models, and future work should expand the scope of interpretability and control to more complex behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns an emergent world representation of the Othello board, and this representation can be intervened on to edit the model's perceived world state.
Inference-time intervention (ITI) can elicit more truthful answers from language models by shifting activations along truthful directions found in attention heads.
Instruction drift in long conversations is caused by attention decay, and split-softmax can mitigate this drift by forcing the model to pay more attention to the system prompt.
Dialogue action tokens (DAT) enable better planning in multi-turn dialogues by using a planner to predict action vectors that steer the language model towards long-horizon goals.
papers.abstract: This dissertation talks about mechanistic control of large language models (LLM). The intuition is that, in order to rigorously control large language models, it is beneficial to first understand their inner working mechanisms. Even though a fully mechanistic understanding of language models is far from complete at the time this dissertation is written, I will demonstrate several cases where such understanding provides a useful surface for control. I argue that connecting interpretability to real-life applications--e.g., alignment and safety--offers advantages to the development of both fields. I first position this methodological approach within a broader scientific context, discussing and systematizing the role of interpretability in artificial intelligence research. I then present four intensive case studies, each leveraging certain interpretability insights to control the behavior of language models. The interpretability insights I explored span emergent world representations, representation of internal knowledge, phenomenon of attention decay, and representation of users. The demonstrated effects of control include targeted editing of the world model, reduced hallucination, improved stability of system prompts in long conversations, and better planning in multi-turn dialogue.

papers.title: Shifting Perspectives: Steering Vectors for Robust Bias Mitigation in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can steering vectors effectively mitigate social biases in LLMs, and how do they compare to other bias mitigation methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that steering vectors, applied to model activations at inference time, are a lightweight and effective method for mitigating social biases in LLMs, outperforming prompting and Self-Debias with minimal impact on general model performance.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors offer a plug-and-play, interpretable, and computationally lightweight intervention for bias mitigation, achieving substantial bias reduction with minimal impact on core LLM performance.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors achieved average accuracy improvements of 12.8% on BBQ, 8.3% on CLEAR-Bias, and 1% on StereoSet.
Steering vectors outperformed prompting and Self-Debias in all cases, and outperformed fine-tuning in 12 out of 17 evaluations.
Steering vectors had the lowest negative impact on MMLU scores (3.9% decrease) compared to other bias mitigation methods tested.
Steering vectors trained on one bias-specific dataset (BBQ) transferred effectively to other tasks and datasets, demonstrating robustness and generalizability.
Linear separability analysis identified optimal intervention layers (13-14) for applying the steering vectors.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on a 7B parameter model, which may not fully capture emergent abilities related to bias observed in larger models.
MMLU may not capture all aspects of language understanding and reasoning; additional benchmarks would provide a more complete assessment.
future_direction: Explore different contrastive dataset structures for constructing steering vectors.
Investigate multi-dimensional steering by controlling along multiple PCA axes simultaneously.
Study cross-axis interactions (e.g., gender vs. race) to mitigate unintended cross-bias amplification.
Develop adaptive coefficient selection strategies to dynamically adjust steering strength per input.
Apply steering vectors to other forms of harmful behaviors (e.g., toxicity, misinformation) and assess real-world impact.
papers.abstract: We present a novel approach to bias mitigation in large language models (LLMs) by applying steering vectors to modify model activations in forward passes. We compute 8 steering vectors, each corresponding to a different social bias axis, such as age, gender, or race, on a training subset of the BBQ dataset and compare the effectiveness of these to 3 additional bias mitigation methods across 4 datasets. When optimized on the BBQ dataset, our individually tuned steering vectors achieve average improvements of 12.8% on BBQ, 8.3% on CLEAR-Bias, and 1% on StereoSet, and show improvements over prompting and Self-Debias in all cases, and improvements over fine-tuning in 12 out of 17 evaluations. In addition, steering vectors showed the lowest impact on MMLU scores of the four bias mitigation methods tested. The work presents the first systematic investigation of steering vectors for bias mitigation, and we demonstrate that they are a powerful and computationally efficient strategy for reducing bias in LLMs, with broader implications for enhancing AI safety.

papers.title: Linear Personality Probing and Steering in LLMs: A Big Five Study
papers.research_question: Whether linear directions aligned with the Big Five personality traits can be used for probing and steering model behavior in large language models.
papers.core_contribution: Linear directions aligned with Big Five traits are effective for personality probing, but steering is context-dependent, working well in forced-choice tasks but limited in open-ended generation or when prompt context is present.
papers.conclusion: Personality-related signals are embedded in the model's representational geometry, but steering vectors show strong context-dependency and are easily overridden by prompt context.
papers.key_findings:
Linear directions derived from regression align with Big Five traits and generalize to trait-relevant adjectives.
Steering with these vectors reliably shifts responses in forced-choice personality assessments.
Steering effects are overridden by explicit personality cues in the prompt.
Steering has minimal effect in open-ended generation tasks.
Regression-derived directions are more effective than SVD-derived directions for steering.
papers.limitation:
Steering effects are overridden by explicit personality cues in the prompt.
Steering is difficult to measure in open-ended generation where clear evaluation metrics are unavailable.
Aggregation across items and characters may obscure personality signals.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit distinct and consistent personalities that greatly impact trust and engagement. While this means that personality frameworks would be highly valuable tools to characterize and control LLMs' behavior, current approaches remain either costly (post-training) or brittle (prompt engineering). Probing and steering via linear directions has recently emerged as a cheap and efficient alternative. In this paper, we investigate whether linear directions aligned with the Big Five personality traits can be used for probing and steering model behavior. Using Llama 3.3 70B, we generate descriptions of 406 fictional characters and their Big Five trait scores. We then prompt the model with these descriptions and questions from the Alpaca questionnaire, allowing us to sample hidden activations that vary along personality traits in known, quantifiable ways. Using linear regression, we learn a set of per-layer directions in activation space, and test their effectiveness for probing and steering model behavior. Our results suggest that linear directions aligned with trait-scores are effective probes for personality detection, while their steering capabilities strongly depend on context, producing reliable effects in forced-choice tasks but limited influence in open-ended generation or when additional context is present in the prompt.

papers.title: How Do LLMs Persuade? Linear Probes Can Uncover Persuasion Dynamics in Multi-Turn Conversations
papers.research_question: How do LLMs persuade in multi-turn conversations? The paper investigates using linear probes to uncover persuasion dynamics, including persuasion success, persuadee personality, and persuasion strategy.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for analyzing persuasion dynamics in LLM-driven conversations using linear probes, demonstrating that these lightweight probes can efficiently capture key aspects of persuasion (outcome, strategy, personality) and match or outperform prompting-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Linear probes are a promising, efficient tool for studying complex behaviors like persuasion in multi-turn LLM conversations, enabling fine-grained analysis at scale and offering insights into persuasion dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can accurately identify where persuasion success or failure occurs in a conversation, detect rhetorical strategies, and estimate persuadee personality.
Probes are computationally much more efficient than prompting-based methods, especially for fine-grained, multi-turn analysis.
Persuasive cues concentrate around the middle turns in human-human dialogues but shift to the final turns in synthetic LLM-generated dialogues.
Probe outputs reveal correlations between personality traits (e.g., extraversion) and the effectiveness of different rhetorical strategies.
Probes can perform as well as or even outperform prompting in some settings, such as uncovering persuasion strategy.
future_direction: Applying the probing approach to study other complex behaviours such as deception and manipulation.
Scaling the approach to larger models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have started to demonstrate the ability to persuade humans, yet our understanding of how this dynamic transpires is limited. Recent work has used linear probes, lightweight tools for analyzing model representations, to study various LLM skills such as the ability to model user sentiment and political perspective. Motivated by this, we apply probes to study persuasion dynamics in natural, multi-turn conversations. We leverage insights from cognitive science to train probes on distinct aspects of persuasion: persuasion success, persuadee personality, and persuasion strategy. Despite their simplicity, we show that they capture various aspects of persuasion at both the sample and dataset levels. For instance, probes can identify the point in a conversation where the persuadee was persuaded or where persuasive success generally occurs across the entire dataset. We also show that in addition to being faster than expensive prompting-based approaches, probes can do just as well and even outperform prompting in some settings, such as when uncovering persuasion strategy. This suggests probes as a plausible avenue for studying other complex behaviours such as deception and manipulation, especially in multi-turn settings and large-scale dataset analysis where prompting-based methods would be computationally inefficient.

papers.title: Gender Encoding Patterns in Pretrained Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: How do pretrained language models internally represent and propagate gender biases? How do bias mitigation techniques and fine-tuning affect these encoded biases?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a consistent pattern of gender encoding in pretrained language models (early layers suppress, later layers amplify) and shows that debiasing techniques, especially post-hoc methods, are limited in altering internal representations, while fine-tuning reduces encoded gender information but may concentrate bias in the classification layer.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that gender bias is deeply embedded in pretrained language models and that current debiasing techniques are insufficient, advocating for proactive integration of fairness objectives during pretraining and targeted interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Gender information follows a consistent encoding pattern across encoder models: early layers suppress gender signals, while later layers amplify them.
Debiasing techniques, especially post-hoc methods, show limited efficacy in reducing encoded gender bias in internal representations.
Training-time Counterfactual Data Augmentation (CDA) is the most effective debiasing method for reducing gender encoding.
Fine-tuning on a downstream task (occupation classification) reduces gender information in the encoder representations, but may concentrate bias in the classification layer.
Larger models (e.g., BERT-large) tend to encode more gender information than smaller models.
papers.limitation:
Focus on gender bias in English-language biographies, leaving broader sociocultural and intersectional biases unexplored.
The study centers on encoder-based models; future work should validate findings in decoder-based architectures and multimodal systems.
The interplay between task-specific fine-tuning and bias propagation requires deeper exploration across diverse applications.
future_direction: Extend analysis to broader sociocultural and intersectional biases.
Validate findings in decoder-based architectures and multimodal systems.
Explore the interplay between fine-tuning and bias propagation across diverse applications.
papers.abstract: Gender bias in pretrained language models (PLMs) poses significant social and ethical challenges.Despite growing awareness, there is a lack of comprehensive investigation into how different models internally represent and propagate such biases.This study adopts an information-theoretic approach to analyze how gender biases are encoded within various encoder-based architectures.We focus on three key aspects: identifying how models encode gender information and biases, examining the impact of bias mitigation techniques and fine-tuning on the encoded biases and their effectiveness, and exploring how model design differences influence the encoding of biases.Through rigorous and systematic investigation, our findings reveal a consistent pattern of gender encoding across diverse models.Surprisingly, debiasing techniques often exhibit limited efficacy, sometimes inadvertently increasing the encoded bias in internal representations while reducing bias in model output distributions.This highlights a disconnect between mitigating bias in output distributions and addressing its internal representations.This work provides valuable guidance for advancing bias mitigation strategies and fostering the development of more equitable language models. 1

papers.title: Belief Dynamics Reveal the Dual Nature of In-Context Learning and Activation Steering
papers.research_question: Whether in-context learning and activation steering are instances of a broader framework for controlling LLM behavior, and how they jointly affect model behavior.
papers.core_contribution: Presents a Bayesian belief dynamics model that unifies in-context learning and activation steering, accurately predicting LLM behavior under both interventions.
papers.conclusion: The Bayesian belief dynamics model unifies in-context learning and activation steering, accurately predicting LLM behavior and revealing a phase boundary between interventions.
papers.key_findings:
In-context learning and activation steering jointly affect behavior, creating a phase boundary modulated by context and activations.
The Bayesian model predicts sigmoidal learning curves as in-context evidence accumulates and additivity of interventions in log-belief space.
The model predicts crossover points (N*) where behavior transitions between concepts, with high correlation to empirical data.
The linear representation hypothesis holds within a range of steering magnitudes, beyond which behavior breaks down.
The model generalizes across different LLMs (Llama, Gemma, Qwen) and datasets (persona, sentiment).
papers.limitation: The linear representation hypothesis breaks down with large steering magnitudes, leading to chance behavior.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can be controlled at inference time through prompts (in-context learning) and internal activations (activation steering). Different accounts have been proposed to explain these methods, yet their common goal of controlling model behavior raises the question of whether these seemingly disparate methodologies can be seen as specific instances of a broader framework. Motivated by this, we develop a unifying, predictive account of LLM control from a Bayesian perspective. Specifically, we posit that both context- and activation-based interventions impact model behavior by altering its belief in latent concepts: steering operates by changing concept priors, while in-context learning leads to an accumulation of evidence. This results in a closed-form Bayesian model that is highly predictive of LLM behavior across context- and activation-based interventions in a set of domains inspired by prior work on many-shot in-context learning. This model helps us explain prior empirical phenomena - e.g., sigmoidal learning curves as in-context evidence accumulates - while predicting novel ones - e.g., additivity of both interventions in log-belief space, which results in distinct phases such that sudden and dramatic behavioral shifts can be induced by slightly changing intervention controls. Taken together, this work offers a unified account of prompt-based and activation-based control of LLM behavior, and a methodology for empirically predicting the effects of these interventions.

papers.title: What Can We Actually Steer? A Multi-Behavior Study of Activation Control
papers.research_question: How does activation steering effectiveness vary across different behavior types, and can the nature of target behaviors predict steering success?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering effectiveness varies significantly by behavior type, with internal traits like personality and misalignment being more steerable than knowledge-dependent behaviors, and vector separation does not predict success.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering is not a universal control method but a semantic modulator effective for abstract, internal dispositions but ineffective for knowledge-heavy roleplay or precise formatting tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Steering effectiveness bifurcates between internal traits (e.g., personality, misalignment) and external knowledge (e.g., public figures), with internal traits being more steerable.
Trait expression follows an inverted-U curve with steering coefficient strength, peaking at moderate coefficients while coherence and relevance decline monotonically.
Vector separation metrics do not predict steering success, contradicting the intuition that larger activation differences yield better control.
Larger training datasets enable more aggressive steering without coherence collapse, improving steering quality despite smaller raw activation differences.
Misalignment behaviors such as hallucination and sycophancy are highly steerable, indicating potential safety risks where adversarial actors could easily amplify harmful traits.
papers.limitation:
Experiments primarily used Llama 3.1 8B, and steerability may scale non-linearly with model size.
Steering was restricted to Layer 15, and different behaviors might be localized at different layers.
Reliance on LLM-as-a-Judge (GPT-4.1) for evaluation introduces potential biases in scoring.
future_direction: Future work should explore whether more sophisticated vector diagnostics or non-linear relationships might better predict steerability.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) require precise behavior control for safe and effective deployment across diverse applications. Activation steering offers a promising approach for LLMs' behavioral control. We focus on the question of how steering effectiveness varies across different behavior types and whether the nature of target behaviors can predict steering success. We address this through empirical analysis of activation steering across 50 behaviors that span persona archetypes, personality traits, misalignment behaviors, style cues, and impersonation of public figures. We present a set of comprehensive experiments on coefficient optimization, vector properties, and data requirements to provide comprehensive guidance for the implementation of activation steering. Our analysis demonstrates that steering effectiveness varies significantly by behavior type, with different behavioral categories exhibiting distinct response patterns to intervention strength. We find that trait expression follows an inverted-U curve with a steering coefficient strength. We also show that vector separation metrics do not predict steering success, but larger training datasets enable more aggressive steering. These findings provide empirically grounded guidance for implementing activation steering and demonstrate that steering effectiveness is heavily influenced by behavior type.

papers.title: Scaling laws for activation steering with Llama 2 models and refusal mechanisms
papers.research_question: How does the effectiveness of the Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) steering technique scale with model size, specifically for controlling refusal behavior in Llama 2 models?
papers.core_contribution: The effectiveness of Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) for steering model behavior diminishes with increasing model size, negative steering is more effective than positive steering, and steering is most effective when applied at early-mid layers.
papers.conclusion: Model alignment is complex and requires nuanced approaches to steer models effectively as they become larger, with future research needed to understand the interplay between alignment strategies, model architecture, and dataset characteristics.
papers.key_findings:
CAA is most effective when applied at early-mid layers (approximately 0.4 × total layer count).
The effectiveness of CAA diminishes with model size, making larger models harder to steer with the same vectors.
Negative steering (towards non-refusal) has more pronounced effects than positive steering across all model sizes.
The layer of peak steering effectiveness for positive and negative steering converges as model size increases.
The diminishing effectiveness might be because larger models 'drown out' the steering vector due to more downstream computation.
papers.limitation: The experiments were limited to the specific topic of refusal and the results may be different for different topics or prompting approaches.
future_direction: Feature steering with sparse autoencoders (SAE).
Modifying activation steering for larger models, e.g., scaling up steering vectors or injecting at multiple layers.
Experimenting with diverse model architectures (e.g., Mistral, BERT, BLOOM) to understand alignment differences.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) evolve in complexity and capability, the efficacy of less widely deployed alignment techniques are uncertain. Building on previous work on activation steering and contrastive activation addition (CAA), this paper explores the effectiveness of CAA with model scale using the family of Llama 2 models (7B, 13B, and 70B). CAA works by finding desirable 'directions' in the model's residual stream vector space using contrastive pairs (for example, hate to love) and adding this direction to the residual stream during the forward pass. It directly manipulates the residual stream and aims to extract features from language models to better control their outputs. Using answer matching questions centered around the refusal behavior, we found that 1) CAA is most effective when applied at early-mid layers. 2) The effectiveness of CAA diminishes with model size. 3) Negative steering has more pronounced effects than positive steering across all model sizes.

papers.title: How Does Controllability Emerge In Language Models During Pretraining?
papers.research_question: How does linear steerability emerge in language models during pretraining, and why does it vary across concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Linear steerability emerges during intermediate stages of training, varies across concepts, and is linked to increasing linear separability of concepts in the hidden space.
papers.conclusion: Linear steerability does not emerge uniformly but develops over training and varies between concepts, aligning with increasingly structured internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Linear steerability emerges in later training stages, separate from reasoning capability and emotion expression via prompting.
Emergence times vary widely across concepts, such as anger emerging earlier than sadness.
Concept representations become increasingly linearly separable in the hidden space as training progresses.
The Intervention Detector (ID) framework can reveal steerability dynamics and predict when linear steerability emerges.
These findings hold across different model families, indicating a general pattern.
papers.limitation:
Only evaluated on 7B-scale open-source models, not tested on larger LLMs.
Intervention coefficient was empirically tuned and differs across models, with underlying causes not investigated.
Did not explore alternative nonlinear approaches for extracting or intervening in model representations.
Methodological innovation in intervention techniques is not the focus; core procedure is consistent with prior work.
Alternative unsupervised methods such as mean-difference vectors are not compared.
Concepts like emotions lack ground truth, making evaluation subjective and based on semantic interpretation.
Steering certain concepts can produce offensive outputs, with no safety filtering applied.
future_direction: Examining how different pre-training corpora influence intervention outcomes.
Exploring alternative steering methods beyond PCA or K-Means.
Comparing unsupervised methods like mean-difference vectors and their influence on downstream intervention performance.
papers.abstract: Language models can be steered by modifying their internal representations to control concepts such as emotion, style, or truthfulness in generation. However, the conditions for an effective intervention remain unclear and are often validated through heuristics and trial-and-error. To fill this gap, we demonstrate that intervention efficacy, measured by linear steerability (i.e., the ability to adjust output via linear transformations of hidden states), emerges during intermediate stages of training. Moreover, even closely related concepts (e.g., anger and sadness) exhibit steerability emergence at distinct stages of training. To better interpret the dynamics of steerability during training, we adapt existing intervention techniques into a unified framework, referred to as the "Intervention Detector" (ID), which is designed to reveal how linear steerability evolves over the course of training through hidden state and representation analysis. ID reveals that concepts become increasingly linearly separable in the hidden space as training progresses, which strongly correlates with the emergence of linear steerability. We further introduce ID-based metrics, such as heatmaps, entropy trends, and cosine similarity, to help interpret how linear steerability evolves throughout training. In addition, we apply ID across different model families to ensure the generality of our findings on steerability dynamics.

papers.title: Steering Towards Fairness: Mitigating Political Bias in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can political bias in decoder-based large language models be mitigated through analysis of internal representations and steering vector-based interventions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for mitigating political bias in LLMs using steering vector ensembles derived from contrastive prompts, demonstrating effective bias reduction while preserving response quality and providing insights into bias encoding in internal representations.
papers.conclusion: Proposes a practical method to reduce political bias in LLMs using contrastive prompts from the Political Compass Test, with Steering Vector Ensembles (SVE) outperforming Individual Steering Vectors (ISV) and providing a foundation for fairer multilingual language models.
papers.key_findings:
Steering Vector Ensembles (SVE) outperform Individual Steering Vectors (ISV) for social bias mitigation, achieving up to 60% reduction on socially framed prompts.
Mid-level transformer layers (e.g., layers 8, 12, 16, 20, 24) encode the strongest ideological signals, making them effective targets for steering interventions.
Bias reduction is most effective at a steering strength of α=1.0, with performance declining beyond this point due to over-correction or destabilization.
SVE maintains response quality and coherence better than ISV, particularly in social bias scenarios, while ISV shows moderate gains on economic prompts.
The method generalizes across models and languages, with DeepSeek benefiting more from SVE and Mistral aligning slightly better with ISV on economic axes.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on Political Compass Test (PCT) statements constrains generalizability to other domains.
Steering strength parameter (α) and layer selection were manually tuned, limiting adaptability across models.
Modifying only the last-token activation may not sufficiently propagate steering in longer generations.
Evaluation relies on keyword-based lexicons, which may miss subtle discursive bias.
Challenges in low-resource settings, such as reduced quality in Punjabi economic prompts due to sparse vocabulary.
future_direction: Explore language-specific calibration to improve robustness in low-resource languages.
Investigate multi-axis steering to handle entanglement between social and economic biases.
Develop stance-conditional methods to balance neutrality with context-appropriate stances.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have enabled their widespread use across diverse real-world applications. However, concerns remain about their tendency to encode and reproduce ideological biases along political and economic dimensions. In this paper, we employ a framework for probing and mitigating such biases in decoder-based LLMs through analysis of internal model representations. Grounded in the Political Compass Test (PCT), this method uses contrastive pairs to extract and compare hidden layer activations from models like Mistral and DeepSeek. We introduce a comprehensive activation extraction pipeline capable of layer-wise analysis across multiple ideological axes, revealing meaningful disparities linked to political framing. Our results show that decoder LLMs systematically encode representational bias across layers, which can be leveraged for effective steering vector-based mitigation. This work provides new insights into how political bias is encoded in LLMs and offers a principled approach to debiasing beyond surface-level output interventions.

papers.title: Mitigating Content Effects on Reasoning in Language Models through Fine-Grained Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How can content biases in reasoning be mitigated through activation steering in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces K-CAST, a fine-grained conditional activation steering method that effectively reduces content biases in reasoning, improving formal reasoning accuracy by up to 15%.
papers.conclusion: Activation-level interventions offer a scalable inference-time strategy for enhancing the robustness of LLMs, contributing towards more systematic and unbiased reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive steering methods enable linear control over content biases in reasoning.
Static steering is insufficient to debias all tested models.
K-CAST reduces biases on unresponsive models, achieving up to 15% absolute improvement in formal reasoning accuracy.
Steering for content effects is robust to prompt variations and incurs minimal side effects on multilingual language modeling capabilities.
Steering vectors can partially generalize to different out-of-distribution reasoning tasks.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are performed on LLMs of up to 9 billion parameters due to computational constraints.
The study focuses mainly on synthetically generated tasks, which may not fully capture real-world applications.
future_direction: Applying the steering methodology to larger models.
Assessing how steering for content effect can impact real-world applications in critical domains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently demonstrate reasoning limitations, often conflating content plausibility (i.e., material inference) with logical validity (i.e., formal inference). This can result in biased inferences, where plausible arguments are incorrectly deemed logically valid or vice versa. Mitigating this limitation is critical, as it undermines the trustworthiness and generalizability of LLMs in applications that demand rigorous logical consistency. This paper investigates the problem of mitigating content biases on formal reasoning through activation steering. Specifically, we curate a controlled syllogistic reasoning dataset to disentangle formal validity from content plausibility. After localising the layers responsible for formal and material inference, we investigate contrastive activation steering methods for test-time interventions. An extensive empirical analysis on different LLMs reveals that contrastive steering consistently supports linear control over content biases. However, we observe that a static approach is insufficient for improving all the tested models. We then leverage the possibility to control content effects by dynamically determining the value of the steering parameters via fine-grained conditional methods. We found that conditional steering is effective on unresponsive models, achieving up to 15% absolute improvement in formal reasoning accuracy with a newly introduced kNN-based method (K-CAST). Finally, additional experiments reveal that steering for content effects is robust to prompt variations, incurs minimal side effects on language modeling capabilities, and can partially generalize to out-of-distribution reasoning tasks. Practically, this paper demonstrates that activation-level interventions can offer a scalable strategy for enhancing the robustness of LLMs, contributing towards more systematic and unbiased formal reasoning.

papers.title: Dual Mechanisms of Value Expression: Intrinsic vs. Prompted Values in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the similarities and differences between intrinsic and prompted value mechanisms in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that intrinsic and prompted value mechanisms in LLMs share common components for value expression but have unique elements that lead to differences in response diversity and steerability.
papers.conclusion: The findings demonstrate that while intrinsic and prompted mechanisms share commonalities, each possesses distinct components that serve different roles, clarifying when to prefer intrinsic versus prompted mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Intrinsic and prompted value mechanisms exhibit nontrivial overlap at both the vector and neuron levels.
Shared components are crucial for value expression and generalize across languages, reconstructing theoretical inter-value correlations.
Intrinsic-unique components promote lexical diversity in model responses.
Prompted-unique components strengthen instruction compliance and affect tasks like jailbreaking.
Value neurons can be decomposed into shared and unique types with distinct functional roles.
future_direction: Applying the analysis to AI safety applications such as diagnosing instruction-following behavior and improving robustness to undesirable behaviors.
papers.abstract: Large language models can express values in two main ways: (1) intrinsic expression, reflecting the model's inherent values learned during training, and (2) prompted expression, elicited by explicit prompts. Given their widespread use in value alignment, it is paramount to clearly understand their underlying mechanisms, particularly whether they mostly overlap (as one might expect) or rely on distinct mechanisms, but this remains largely understudied. We analyze this at the mechanistic level using two approaches: (1) value vectors, feature directions representing value mechanisms extracted from the residual stream, and (2) value neurons, MLP neurons that contribute to value vectors. We demonstrate that intrinsic and prompted value mechanisms partly share common components crucial for inducing value expression, generalizing across languages and reconstructing theoretical inter-value correlations in the model's internal representations. Yet, as these mechanisms also possess unique elements that fulfill distinct roles, they lead to different degrees of response diversity (intrinsic > prompted) and value steerability (prompted > intrinsic). In particular, components unique to the intrinsic mechanism promote lexical diversity in responses, whereas those specific to the prompted mechanism strengthen instruction following, taking effect even in distant tasks like jailbreaking.

papers.title: Small Vectors, Big Effects: A Mechanistic Study of RL-Induced Reasoning via Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How does reasoning training reshape LLMs' internal computations, and what are the mechanisms of trainable steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Lightweight steering vectors trained with an RL objective explain a large portion of full fine-tuning performance increase while preserving interpretability, and their mechanisms (e.g., token substitution at the last layer, MLP-mediated effects at the penultimate layer) are elucidated.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors provide a compact and informative probe of reasoning-trained models, offering concrete insight into how RL-induced changes manifest in token preferences and internal circuitry.
papers.key_findings:
The last-layer steering vector acts like a token-substitution bias concentrated on the first generated token, boosting tokens such as 'To' and 'Step'.
The penultimate-layer vector leaves attention patterns largely intact and operates through the MLP and unembedding, up-weighting process words and structure symbols.
Steering vectors transfer to other models from the same family, suggesting underlying directions are preserved under fine-tuning.
Early-layer steering does not express later-layer steering directions; induced shifts diffuse and become nearly orthogonal to later-layer vectors.
Single-layer steering vectors isolate layer-specific effects and provide an upper bound on linear intervention performance at that layer.
papers.limitation: The effects are consistently stronger and cleaner in Qwen than in Llama, suggesting model-specific implementations of similar high-level behaviors.
future_direction: Systematic comparisons across architectures and training recipes to explain differences in steering vector effects.
Pin down the precise mechanisms of mid-layer steering vectors, which are harder to localize to a single submodule.
papers.abstract: The mechanisms by which reasoning training reshapes LLMs' internal computations remain unclear. We study lightweight steering vectors inserted into the base model's residual stream and trained with a reinforcement-learning objective. These vectors explain a large portion of full fine-tuning performance increase while preserving the interpretability of small, additive interventions. We find that (i) the last-layer steering vector acts like a token-substitution bias concentrated on the first generated token, consistently boosting tokens such as "To" and "Step"; (ii) the penultimate-layer vector leaves attention patterns largely intact and instead operates through the MLP and unembedding, preferentially up-weighting process words and structure symbols; and (iii) the steering vectors transfer to other models from the same family. Taken together, these results deepen understanding of how trained steering vectors shape computation and should inform future work in activation engineering and the study of reasoning models.

papers.title: Unveiling the "Fairness Seesaw": Discovering and Mitigating Gender and Race Bias in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent do state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs) yield gender and race bias in responses? Do VLMs have reliable confidence levels in different social groups? How can we mitigate these biases?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers the 'Fairness Seesaw' phenomenon in Vision-Language Models and proposes RES-FAIR, a post-hoc method that mitigates gender and race bias by projecting hidden states away from biased residual directions and amplifying fair components.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a new lens for understanding how multi-modal models store and process sensitive social information and demonstrates an effective post-hoc method for bias mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
The Fairness Paradox: Models often generate 'fair' text labels while maintaining highly skewed confidence scores toward specific social groups.
Layer-wise Fluctuation: Fairness knowledge peaks in intermediate layers and undergoes substantial 'knowledge erosion' in the final layers.
Residual Discrepancy: Within a single hidden layer, different residual streams carry conflicting social knowledge—some reinforcing fairness while others amplifying bias.
RES-FAIR significantly improves response fairness and confidence calibration without compromising general reasoning abilities.
State-of-the-art VLMs still struggle to produce fair responses and have mis-calibrated confidence distributions.
papers.limitation: The study of race is limited to 'black' and 'white' categories due to dataset constraints, which is expandable in future work.
future_direction: Expanding the study to include more race labels beyond 'black' and 'white'.
papers.abstract: Although Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable success, the knowledge mechanisms underlying their social biases remain a black box, where fairness- and ethics-related problems harm certain groups of people in society. It is unknown to what extent VLMs yield gender and race bias in generative responses. In this paper, we conduct a systematic discovery of gender and race bias in state-of-the-art VLMs, focusing not only on surface-level responses but also on the internal probability distributions and hidden state dynamics. Our empirical analysis reveals three critical findings: 1) The Fairness Paradox: Models often generate fair text labels while maintaining highly skewed confidence scores (mis-calibration) toward specific social groups. 2) Layer-wise Fluctuation: Fairness knowledge is not uniformly distributed; it peaks in intermediate layers and undergoes substantial knowledge erosion in the final layers. 3) Residual Discrepancy: Within a single hidden layer, different residual streams carry conflicting social knowledge - some reinforcing fairness while others amplifying bias. Leveraging these insights, we propose RES-FAIR (RESidual Flow Adjustment for Inference Recalibration), a post-hoc framework that mitigates bias by localizing and projecting hidden states away from biased residual directions while amplifying fair components. Evaluations on PAIRS and SocialCounterfactuals datasets demonstrate that our discovery-based approach significantly improves response fairness and confidence calibration without compromising general reasoning abilities. Our work provides a new lens for understanding how multi-modal models store and process sensitive social information.

papers.title: Analysing Moral Bias in Finetuned LLMs through Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether LLMs exhibit the Knobe effect (a moral bias in intentionality judgments), whether specific Transformer layers encode this bias, and whether targeted interventions (layer-patching) can mitigate it.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the Knobe effect (a moral bias) emerges in finetuned LLMs, is localized in mid-to-late Transformer layers, and can be mitigated by patching activations from pretrained models into finetuned models, without retraining.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that social biases in LLMs can be mechanistically localized and mitigated through targeted interventions like layer-patching, offering a method for model repair without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Finetuned LLMs exhibit the Knobe effect (moral bias in intentionality judgments), while pretrained models show minimal effect.
The bias is localized in mid-to-late Transformer layers, as shown by differences in residual stream activations.
Patching activations from pretrained models into specific layers of finetuned models can reduce or eliminate the bias.
The mitigation via layer-patching does not significantly harm general model performance on standard benchmarks.
The Knobe effect is not an emergent property of model scale alone; it is induced by finetuning and appears across model sizes.
papers.limitation: The layer-patching method requires access to the pretrained model.
future_direction: Explore whether this localization technique applies to other biases, such as gender or racial stereotypes.
Develop methods that do not rely on access to the pretrained model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to internalize human-like biases during finetuning, yet the mechanisms by which these biases manifest remain unclear. In this work, we investigated whether the well-known Knobe effect, a moral bias in intentionality judgements, emerges in finetuned LLMs and whether it can be traced back to specific components of the model. We conducted a Layer-Patching analysis across 3 open-weights LLMs and demonstrated that the bias is not only learned during finetuning but also localized in a specific set of layers. Surprisingly, we found that patching activations from the corresponding pretrained model into just a few critical layers is sufficient to eliminate the effect. Our findings offer new evidence that social biases in LLMs can be interpreted, localized, and mitigated through targeted interventions, without the need for model retraining.

papers.title: Large Language Models as Psychological Simulators: A Methodological Guide
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a methodological framework and guidelines for using LLMs as psychological simulators in two primary applications: simulating roles/personas and serving as cognitive models, while addressing challenges and ethical considerations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs are tools to augment, not replace, human-centered research, and their effective use requires precision, rigor, and a dual commitment from psychologists and the AI community.
papers.limitation:
LLMs have temporal limitations due to training data cutoffs, preventing them from reflecting events, cultural shifts, or emerging knowledge after the cutoff date.
LLMs exhibit cultural and demographic biases due to overrepresentation of WEIRD populations in training data, which can distort simulations of marginalized groups or non-Western cultures.
LLMs often fail to capture the full range of human psychological diversity, showing more extreme and less nuanced preference distributions compared to human participants.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer emerging opportunities for psychological and behavioral research, but methodological guidance is lacking. This article provides a framework for using LLMs as psychological simulators across two primary applications: simulating roles and personas to explore diverse contexts, and serving as computational models to investigate cognitive processes. For simulation, we present methods for developing psychologically grounded personas that move beyond demographic categories, with strategies for validation against human data and use cases ranging from studying inaccessible populations to prototyping research instruments. For cognitive modeling, we synthesize emerging approaches for probing internal representations, methodological advances in causal interventions, and strategies for relating model behavior to human cognition. We address overarching challenges including prompt sensitivity, temporal limitations from training data cutoffs, and ethical considerations that extend beyond traditional human subjects review. Throughout, we emphasize the need for transparency about model capabilities and constraints. Together, this framework integrates emerging empirical evidence about LLM performance--including systematic biases, cultural limitations, and prompt brittleness--to help researchers wrangle these challenges and leverage the unique capabilities of LLMs in psychological research.

papers.title: What Triggers my Model? Contrastive Explanations Inform Gender Choices by Translation Models
papers.research_question: How to measure attribution levels of source words on machine translation model's gender decisions, which source words are most salient, and to what extent salient words agree with human perceptions.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how contrastive explanations and saliency attribution can be used to understand gender bias in machine translation models, showing high overlap between model-attributed salient words and human annotations, with differences in part-of-speech categories and dependency distances.
papers.conclusion: The study moves beyond measuring bias to exploring its origins by comparing model and human perceptions, highlighting the importance of understanding model behavior for mitigating gender bias in machine translation.
papers.key_findings:
High overlap between model salient words and human annotations, with the best overlap achieved at the top 15% relative attribution threshold.
Nouns and verbs are the most salient part-of-speech categories for the model's gender decisions.
Salient words for the model are typically at a closer dependency distance to the target referent compared to human annotations.
The model predominantly translates gender-ambiguous referents into masculine forms, while human annotations show more variation.
Different approaches to measuring attribution levels yield varying overlaps, with relative attribution scores performing best.
papers.limitation:
The dataset comprising 60 sentences is very small.
Only one model (OPUS-MT) and two language pairs (EN→DE/ES) were tested.
Model tokenization impacts saliency analysis, and subword merging may introduce errors.
There is low inter-annotator agreement in human annotations, indicating variability in human perceptions.
The study focuses on binary gender, excluding non-binary or inclusive translations.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to a larger dataset once available.
Compare different models and languages in future work.
Address the limitation of available open-source models and toolkits for contrastive approaches.
papers.abstract: Interpretability can be implemented as a means to understand decisions taken by (black box) models, such as machine translation (MT) or large language models (LLMs). Yet, research in this area has been limited in relation to a manifested problem in these models: gender bias. With this research, we aim to move away from simply measuring bias to exploring its origins. Working with gender-ambiguous natural source data, this study examines which context, in the form of input tokens in the source sentence, influences (or triggers) the translation model choice of a certain gender inflection in the target language. To analyse this, we use contrastive explanations and compute saliency attribution. We first address the challenge of a lacking scoring threshold and specifically examine different attribution levels of source words on the model gender decisions in the translation. We compare salient source words with human perceptions of gender and demonstrate a noticeable overlap between human perceptions and model attribution. Additionally, we provide a linguistic analysis of salient words. Our work showcases the relevance of understanding model translation decisions in terms of gender, how this compares to human decisions and that this information should be leveraged to mitigate gender bias.

papers.title: Can Role Vectors Affect LLM Behaviour?
papers.research_question: Can we identify role vectors in the activation space that improve performance on objective tasks? Do these directions effectively impersonate the role of interest? Does ablating these directions degrade performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces role vectors, a method to steer LLM behavior by manipulating internal activations, showing that this approach improves in-domain and cross-domain task performance more effectively than persona-based prompting.
papers.conclusion: Role vectors can effectively steer LLM behavior and improve performance on objective tasks, providing a more direct and effective control mechanism than persona-based prompting.
papers.key_findings:
Role vectors can be identified and used to improve performance on domain-specific tasks, with in-domain improvements and unexpected cross-domain gains.
Ablating the role vectors degrades performance, indicating their causal role in the model's behavior.
The effect of role vectors is more consistent and substantial than traditional persona-based prompting.
The results support the linear representation hypothesis, showing that high-level concepts are linearly represented in the activation space.
The method generalizes across multiple models and domains, as shown by cross-dataset validation on MedQA.
papers.abstract: The influence of personas on Large Language Models (LLMs) has been widely studied, yet their direct impact on performance remains uncertain. This work explores a novel approach to guiding LLM behaviour through role vectors, an alternative to persona-based prompting. We construct 29 role vectors derived from model activations and evaluate their impact on benchmark performance across multiple domains. Our analysis investigates whether these vectors can effectively steer models toward domain-specific expertise. We measure two key interventions: (i) activation addition, which reinforces role-specific directions, and (ii) directional ablation, which removes them. Results on well-established benchmarks indicate that role vectors do, in fact, influence model behaviour, improving in-domain task performance while also yielding unexpected cross-domain gains. This, in turn, suggests that manipulating internal model representations has a greater impact on outcomes than persona-based prompting.

papers.title: Designing Role Vectors to Improve LLM Inference Behaviour
papers.research_question: Can we identify specific latent role directions within the activation space that lead to improved performance on objective tasks? Do these directions effectively impersonate the role of interest? Does eliminating these directions degrade performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces role vectors as a method to steer LLM behavior by manipulating internal activations, showing that this can improve performance in domain-specific tasks.
papers.conclusion: Role vectors offer a promising pathway for achieving more controllable behaviour in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Role vectors can steer models to improve performance in target domains.
Larger models show more interpretable role directions.
Only a subset of directions align with intended roles.
Ablating role directions can degrade performance in target domains.
Steering effects are sensitive to model scale and intervention depth.
papers.limitation:
Results might differ in untested models, especially larger ones.
Lack of a complete mechanistic explanation of the phenomenon.
Uncertain semantic interpretation of the identified directions.
Potential degradation in performance in unrelated tasks.
Possible reinforcement of biases or over-confidence.
future_direction: Using Activation Patching (Causal Mediation Analysis) techniques with SAE features to better explain the phenomenon.
Exploring additional analytical dimensions and potential biases.
papers.abstract: The influence of personas on Large Language Models (LLMs) has been widely studied, yet their direct impact on performance remains uncertain. This work explores a novel approach to guiding LLM behaviour through role vectors, an alternative to persona-based prompting. We construct 29 role vectors derived from model activations and evaluate their impact on benchmark performance across multiple domains. Our analysis investigates whether these vectors can effectively steer models toward domain-specific expertise. We measure two key interventions: (i) activation addition, which reinforces role-specific directions, and (ii) directional ablation, which removes them. Results on well-established benchmarks indicate that role vectors do, in fact, influence model behaviour, improving task performance in relevant domains while marginally affecting unrelated tasks. This, in turn, suggests that manipulating internal model representations has a greater impact on outcomes than persona-based prompting.

papers.title: Identifying Cooperative Personalities in Multi-agent Contexts through Personality Steering with Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: How do personality traits, steered via representation engineering, affect LLM behavior and cooperation in multi-agent games like the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma?
papers.core_contribution: Personality steering using representation engineering effectively promotes cooperation in LLM-based multi-agent systems, but with a trade-off between cooperation and vulnerability to exploitation.
papers.conclusion: Personality steering through representation engineering effectively promotes cooperation in LLM-based multi-agent systems, providing a foundation for future work in cooperative AI agents.
papers.key_findings:
Steering towards agreeableness, conscientiousness, and openness reduces troublemaking rates to zero.
High agreeableness increases exploitability, highlighting a trade-off between cooperation and vulnerability.
Agreeableness and conscientiousness lower lying rates, promoting honesty regardless of opponent behavior.
Models steered towards agreeableness and conscientiousness achieve better collective outcomes but worse individual outcomes.
Personality-steered behavior aligns with human psychological traits in similar contexts.
papers.limitation:
Limited to Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma variants and a single payoff matrix.
Effectiveness across different LLM architectures and tasks remains an open question.
Real-world multi-agent interactions involve more complex incentives.
future_direction: Explore diverse game-theoretic frameworks beyond IPD
Validate results across broader contexts and applications
Investigate effectiveness across different LLM architectures
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) gain autonomous capabilities, their coordination in multi-agent settings becomes increasingly important. However, they often struggle with cooperation, leading to suboptimal outcomes. Inspired by Axelrod's Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma (IPD) tournaments, we explore how personality traits influence LLM cooperation. Using representation engineering, we steer Big Five traits (e.g., Agreeableness, Conscientiousness) in LLMs and analyze their impact on IPD decision-making. Our results show that higher Agreeableness and Conscientiousness improve cooperation but increase susceptibility to exploitation, highlighting both the potential and limitations of personality-based steering for aligning AI agents.

papers.title: DISCO: Disentangled Communication Steering for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Is steering the query and value representation spaces within attention heads more effective for controlling LLM behavior than steering attention head outputs or other spaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DISCO Steering, a method that injects steering vectors directly into the query and value spaces of attention heads, providing more granular control and superior performance over existing steering vector baselines.
papers.conclusion: Query and value spaces are powerful building blocks for steering vector methods, and DISCO provides an effective and flexible approach for controlling LLM behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Query and value spaces exhibit higher linear discriminability of concepts compared to attention head outputs.
DISCO Steering disentangles the strong Communication Steering baseline, allowing independent control of query and value steering magnitudes.
DISCO achieves the best performance in 13 out of 16 experiments across multiple datasets and models.
Steering query spaces dynamically re-weights attention, while steering value spaces directly adds to the head output.
The method is effective for promoting and suppressing behaviors like truthfulness, power-seeking, wealth-seeking, and corrigibility.
papers.limitation:
Requires a dataset of positive and negative examples for each concept.
Steering vectors are linear, which may not capture nonlinear concepts.
Could be misused for jailbreaks or generating inappropriate content.
future_direction: Extending DISCO to other model architectures (e.g., encoder-decoder, multimodal).
Exploring nonlinear steering vectors.
Applying DISCO to more complex behaviors and real-world applications.
papers.abstract: A variety of recent methods guide large language model outputs via the inference-time addition of steering vectors to residual-stream or attention-head representations. In contrast, we propose to inject steering vectors directly into the query and value representation spaces within attention heads. We provide evidence that a greater portion of these spaces exhibit high linear discriminability of concepts --a key property motivating the use of steering vectors-- than attention head outputs. We analytically characterize the effect of our method, which we term DISentangled COmmunication (DISCO) Steering, on attention head outputs. Our analysis reveals that DISCO disentangles a strong but underutilized baseline, steering attention inputs, which implicitly modifies queries and values in a rigid manner. In contrast, DISCO's direct modulation of these components enables more granular control. We find that DISCO achieves superior performance over a number of steering vector baselines across multiple datasets on LLaMA 3.1 8B and Gemma 2 9B, with steering efficacy scoring up to 19.1% higher than the runner-up. Our results support the conclusion that the query and value spaces are powerful building blocks for steering vector methods.

papers.title: Intrinsic Self-Correction in LLMs: Towards Explainable Prompting via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: Does intrinsic self-correction prompting act as representation steering along interpretable latent directions?
papers.core_contribution: Intrinsic self-correction in LLMs functions by steering hidden representations along interpretable latent directions, as evidenced by alignment between prompt-induced shifts and steering vectors and causal verification via activation addition.
papers.conclusion: The findings link self-correction prompting to representation steering along interpretable latent directions, highlighting the role of interpretability methods in understanding prompt-driven LLM phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
Prompt-induced shifts in self-correction align with steering vectors constructed from contrastive pairs.
Activation injection with steering vectors causally reproduces behavioral changes in toxicity.
Detoxification is effective even with weak prompts, while toxification requires strong prompts.
Most of the behavioral change occurs in the first self-correction round.
Alignment between shifts and vectors peaks in mid-to-late layers for some models.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to toxicity-related behaviors and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other prompt-driven phenomena such as chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.abstract: Intrinsic self-correction refers to the phenomenon where a language model refines its own outputs purely through prompting, without external feedback or parameter updates. While this approach improves performance across diverse tasks, its mechanism remains unclear. We show that intrinsic self-correction functions by steering hidden representations along interpretable latent directions, as evidenced by both alignment analysis and activation interventions. To achieve this, we analyze intrinsic self-correction via the representation shift induced by prompting. In parallel, we construct interpretable latent directions with contrastive pairs and verify the causal effect of these directions via activation addition. Evaluating six open-source LLMs, our results demonstrate that prompt-induced representation shifts in text detoxification and text toxification consistently align with latent directions constructed from contrastive pairs. In detoxification, the shifts align with the non-toxic direction; in toxification, they align with the toxic direction. These findings suggest that representation steering is the mechanistic driver of intrinsic self-correction. Our analysis highlights that understanding model internals offers a direct route to analyzing the mechanisms of prompt-driven LLM behaviors.

papers.title: Beacon: Single-Turn Diagnosis and Mitigation of Latent Sycophancy in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to diagnose and mitigate latent sycophancy in large language models using a forced-choice benchmark and activation steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Beacon benchmark for diagnosing sycophancy in LLMs and demonstrates the use of activation steering for mitigation.
papers.conclusion: Beacon reframes sycophancy as a measurable form of normative misgeneralization, providing a reproducible foundation for studying and mitigating alignment drift in large-scale generative systems.
papers.key_findings:
Sycophancy decomposes into stable linguistic and affective sub-biases, each scaling with model capacity.
Prompt-level interventions reduce overt sycophantic behavior but have limited impact and can lead to residual errors or shifted failure modes.
