To test this, we construct a well-defined environment with known outcome logic: blackjack. In more than 1,000 trials, we uncover statistically significant evidence suggesting behavioral misalignment in the learned representations of LLM.

papers.title: The Devil is in the Neurons: Interpreting and Mitigating Social Biases in Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: How to precisely identify the social bias neurons in PLMs? How to effectively mitigate social biases in PLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of social bias neurons, proposes Integrated Gap Gradients (IG2) to identify them, and derives Bias Neuron Suppression (BNS) to mitigate social biases in pre-trained language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes IG2 for interpreting social bias neurons and BNS for mitigating social biases, with experimental verification and analysis providing insights for future fairness research.
papers.key_findings:
IG2 accurately pinpoints social bias neurons in PLMs, as verified by suppression and amplification experiments.
Suppressing social bias neurons reduces bias, while amplifying them increases bias.
BNS effectively mitigates social biases while preserving language modeling ability, outperforming baseline methods.
Social bias neurons are concentrated in the deepest layers of BERT and RoBERTa; after debiasing (FairBERTa), they shift to shallower layers.
Different demographic dimensions have varying numbers of social bias neurons, with 'Ethnicity' having the most and 'Gender' the fewest.
papers.limitation: The BNS method directly sets the activation values of selected social bias neurons to zero, which, while effective, might be improved by a more refined suppression method.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained Language models (PLMs) have been acknowledged to contain harmful information, such as social biases, which may cause negative social impacts or even bring catastrophic results in application. Previous works on this problem mainly focused on using black-box methods such as probing to detect and quantify social biases in PLMs by observing model outputs. As a result, previous debiasing methods mainly finetune or even pre-train language models on newly constructed anti-stereotypical datasets, which are high-cost. In this work, we try to unveil the mystery of social bias inside language models by introducing the concept of {\sc Social Bias Neurons}. Specifically, we propose {\sc Integrated Gap Gradients (IG$^2$)} to accurately pinpoint units (i.e., neurons) in a language model that can be attributed to undesirable behavior, such as social bias. By formalizing undesirable behavior as a distributional property of language, we employ sentiment-bearing prompts to elicit classes of sensitive words (demographics) correlated with such sentiments. Our IG$^2$ thus attributes the uneven distribution for different demographics to specific Social Bias Neurons, which track the trail of unwanted behavior inside PLM units to achieve interoperability. Moreover, derived from our interpretable technique, {\sc Bias Neuron Suppression (BNS)} is further proposed to mitigate social biases. By studying BERT, RoBERTa, and their attributable differences from debiased FairBERTa, IG$^2$ allows us to locate and suppress identified neurons, and further mitigate undesired behaviors. As measured by prior metrics from StereoSet, our model achieves a higher degree of fairness while maintaining language modeling ability with low cost.

papers.title: Programming Refusal with Conditional Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How can we conditionally control LLM behavior (e.g., refusal) based on input context using activation steering, without weight optimization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Conditional Activation Steering (CAST), a method that enables fine-grained, context-dependent control over LLM behaviors by using condition vectors to selectively apply behavior vectors during inference, without weight optimization.
papers.conclusion: CAST provides a flexible and efficient way to program refusal behaviors in LLMs by using condition vectors, enabling fine-grained control without weight updates.
papers.key_findings:
CAST enables selective refusal of harmful prompts while maintaining normal responses to harmless ones.
Condition vectors can be logically composed (e.g., OR, AND, NOT) to create complex refusal conditions.
The method exhibits duality (flipping condition direction intervenes on the complement set) and modulation (adjusting threshold changes sensitivity).
CAST is efficient, requiring no weight updates, and performance saturates quickly with data.
The method can induce or suppress refusal behavior for specific fine-grained categories (e.g., hate speech, legal advice).
papers.limitation: The method requires grid search for hyperparameters (threshold, layer, direction) which can be model-dependent and time-consuming.
papers.abstract: LLMs have shown remarkable capabilities, but precisely controlling their response behavior remains challenging. Existing activation steering methods alter LLM behavior indiscriminately, limiting their practical applicability in settings where selective responses are essential, such as content moderation or domain-specific assistants. In this paper, we propose Conditional Activation Steering (CAST), which analyzes LLM activation patterns during inference to selectively apply or withhold activation steering based on the input context. Our method is based on the observation that different categories of prompts activate distinct patterns in the model's hidden states. Using CAST, one can systematically control LLM behavior with rules like "if input is about hate speech or adult content, then refuse" or "if input is not about legal advice, then refuse." This allows for selective modification of responses to specific content while maintaining normal responses to other content, all without requiring weight optimization. We release an open-source implementation of our framework at github.com/IBM/activation-steering .

papers.title: Robust Concept Erasure Using Task Vectors
papers.research_question: How to unconditionally erase a concept from a text-to-image model to make it robust to unexpected user inputs, and how to estimate the required edit strength for task vector-based erasure?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Diverse Inversion to estimate the required strength of task vector edits for robust concept erasure, enabling input-independent erasure that better maintains model utility.
papers.conclusion: TV-based erasure with Diverse Inversion provides robust concept erasure independent of user prompts and maintains model utility, with potential extension to other model families.
papers.key_findings:
TV-based concept erasure is more robust to unexpected user inputs compared to input-dependent methods like fine-tuning.
Diverse Inversion allows better estimation of the edit strength parameter α by finding a diverse set of adversarial prompts.
Pruning the task vector to edit only a subset of model weights (e.g., first few UNet blocks) can improve the trade-off between erasure and control task performance.
papers.limitation:
Provable guarantees for erasure are not possible against unknown future adversarial methods.
TV-based erasure depends on the parameter space understanding, and its applicability to fine-grained concepts is unclear.
The method depends on the Diverse Inversion set for hyperparameter tuning, though the edit itself is independent.
future_direction: Extending the method to large language models (LLMs) and other multimodal vision-language models.
Applying Diverse Inversion techniques to other modalities such as language.
papers.abstract: With the rapid growth of text-to-image models, a variety of techniques have been suggested to prevent undesirable image generations. Yet, these methods often only protect against specific user prompts and have been shown to allow unsafe generations with other inputs. Here we focus on unconditionally erasing a concept from a text-to-image model rather than conditioning the erasure on the user's prompt. We first show that compared to input-dependent erasure methods, concept erasure that uses Task Vectors (TV) is more robust to unexpected user inputs, not seen during training. However, TV-based erasure can also affect the core performance of the edited model, particularly when the required edit strength is unknown. To this end, we propose a method called Diverse Inversion, which we use to estimate the required strength of the TV edit. Diverse Inversion finds within the model input space a large set of word embeddings, each of which induces the generation of the target concept. We find that encouraging diversity in the set makes our estimation more robust to unexpected prompts. Finally, we show that Diverse Inversion enables us to apply a TV edit only to a subset of the model weights, enhancing the erasure capabilities while better maintaining the core functionality of the model.

papers.title: Feature Steering for Reliable and Expressive AI Engineering
papers.research_question: How does feature steering differ from prompting and fine-tuning, and why can it provide more reliable and expressive control over AI models?
papers.core_contribution: Feature steering is introduced as a method for reliable and expressive AI engineering by directly modifying model internals using features, overcoming limitations of black-box methods like prompting and fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Neuron programming through feature steering is presented as the future for enabling safe and reliable AI systems by allowing engineers to open up model internals for better control.
papers.key_findings:
Feature steering allows nuanced control over model behavior, such as adjusting conciseness strength continuously, unlike binary prompting.
It enables efficient persona management by dynamically adjusting features for different user segments without maintaining separate prompts.
Feature steering opens up novel user interactions, like sliders for communication preferences or adjusting image and music attributes.
It supports deep customization quickly, such as creating characters or brand voices, which would take months with fine-tuning.
Feature steering can be applied conditionally, activating behaviors based on context, like offering discounts when a customer is angry.
papers.limitation: Feature steering cannot introduce new knowledge into the model; for that, fine-tuning is necessary.
papers.abstract: How does feature steering differ from prompting and fine-tuning, and why can it provide more reliable and expressive control over AI models? Feature steering is introduced as a method for reliable and expressive AI engineering by directly modifying model internals using features, overcoming limitations of black-box methods like prompting and fine-tuning. Neuron programming through feature steering is presented as the future for enabling safe and reliable AI systems by allowing engineers to open up model internals for better control.

papers.title: Are the Values of LLMs Structurally Aligned with Humans? A Causal Perspective
papers.research_question: Are the internal value structures of LLMs causally aligned with human value systems?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs have latent causal value graphs that differ from human value systems, and these graphs can guide lightweight value-steering methods (role-based prompting and SAE steering) to mitigate unexpected side effects.
papers.conclusion: The internal value mechanisms of LLMs remain significantly different from humans despite alignment training; leveraging causal value graphs to guide role-based prompting and SAE steering mitigates side effects, with SAE offering fine-grained modulation.
papers.key_findings:
The internal value structures of LLMs, captured by causal graphs, are significantly different from human value systems like Schwartz's theory.
Causal value graphs can effectively predict the effects of value steering, reducing unexpected side effects.
SAE steering provides more fine-grained and precise control over value dimensions than role-based prompting, affecting fewer source nodes.
SAE steering is effective, as shown by consistency within QAs and within values.
LLMs do not always follow explicit value instructions effectively, and SAE steering can have advantages over explicit instructions.
papers.limitation:
The ValueBench dataset offers a uniform approach to value assessment with relatively few questions per value, limiting causal inferences across a wider range of dimensions.
Future research could explore larger versions of LLMs to investigate alignment with the intricate structure of human values.
future_direction: Explore expanding experiments to incorporate larger versions of LLMs and investigate alignment with diverse human value structures.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly integrated into critical applications, aligning their behavior with human values presents significant challenges. Current methods, such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), typically focus on a limited set of coarse-grained values and are resource-intensive. Moreover, the correlations between these values remain implicit, leading to unclear explanations for value-steering outcomes. Our work argues that a latent causal value graph underlies the value dimensions of LLMs and that, despite alignment training, this structure remains significantly different from human value systems. We leverage these causal value graphs to guide two lightweight value-steering methods: role-based prompting and sparse autoencoder (SAE) steering, effectively mitigating unexpected side effects. Furthermore, SAE provides a more fine-grained approach to value steering. Experiments on Gemma-2B-IT and Llama3-8B-IT demonstrate the effectiveness and controllability of our methods.

papers.title: Who's asking? User personas and the mechanics of latent misalignment
papers.research_question: How does the user persona affect the refusal behavior of safety-tuned language models, and what are the underlying mechanisms of latent misalignment?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that safety filters in language models can be manipulated via user persona steering, revealing that harmful content persists in early layers and that safety tuning induces layerwise safeguards rather than eliminating misaligned capabilities globally.
papers.conclusion: User persona is a significant factor in latent misalignment, and safety mechanisms are localized in later layers; geometric measures can predict persona effects.
papers.key_findings:
User persona manipulation via activation steering is more effective than natural language prompting in eliciting harmful content from safety-tuned models.
Safety tuning does not eliminate misaligned capabilities uniformly; harmful information persists in early layers and can be extracted by early decoding.
The effectiveness of persona steering vectors is layer-dependent, with mid-layers (e.g., layer 13) being most effective.
The geometry of steering vectors (cosine similarity) reflects the processing stages of the transformer and can predict downstream effects on refusal.
Persona interventions selectively impact adversarial queries, while prompt prefixes induce refusal across both adversarial and non-adversarial queries.
papers.limitation:
Only a subset of harmful behaviors is studied.
The study is limited to a few models.
Automatic evaluation may not perfectly align with human judgment.
Geometric analysis relies on cosine similarity, which has limitations for measuring semantic similarity.
future_direction: Explore a broader range of harmful behaviors and more models.
Investigate the relationship between persona and other model behaviors.
Develop more robust evaluation methods.
papers.abstract: Despite investments in improving model safety, studies show that misaligned capabilities remain latent in safety-tuned models. In this work, we shed light on the mechanics of this phenomenon. First, we show that even when model generations are safe, harmful content can persist in hidden representations and can be extracted by decoding from earlier layers. Then, we show that whether the model divulges such content depends significantly on its perception of who it is talking to, which we refer to as user persona. In fact, we find manipulating user persona to be even more effective for eliciting harmful content than direct attempts to control model refusal. We study both natural language prompting and activation steering as control methods and show that activation steering is significantly more effective at bypassing safety filters. We investigate why certain personas break model safeguards and find that they enable the model to form more charitable interpretations of otherwise dangerous queries. Finally, we show we can predict a persona's effect on refusal given only the geometry of its steering vector.

papers.title: Comparing Bottom-Up and Top-Down Steering Approaches on In-Context Learning Tasks
papers.research_question: What is the comparative effectiveness of bottom-up (function vectors) and top-down (in-context vectors) steering approaches on diverse in-context learning tasks, and under what conditions does each method excel?
papers.core_contribution: Bottom-up function vectors excel at precise functional tasks but struggle with behavioral shifts, while top-down in-context vectors are effective for behavioral shifts but less reliable for precise tasks, highlighting complementary strengths and limitations of the two steering approaches.
papers.conclusion: Both bottom-up and top-down steering methods are effective only on specific types of in-context learning tasks and cannot fully replace in-context learning, highlighting the need for a unified evaluation benchmark and better understanding of in-context learning mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Function vectors (FVs) outperform in-context vectors (ICVs) on all functional tasks (antonym, capitalize, country-capital, synonym) across zero-shot, few-shot, and natural text settings.
In-context vectors (ICVs) outperform function vectors (FVs) on behavioral tasks (detoxification, sentiment transfer), but with high variance and sensitivity to demonstration data.
ICVs are prone to causing fluency degradation and are less robust when applied in different contexts, while FVs generalize better to out-of-distribution settings.
FV performance is strongly correlated with the causal indirect effect (CIE) of attention heads, indicating that FVs rely on the existence of attention heads that significantly affect task performance.
Both steering methods have significant limitations and cannot serve as a general substitute for in-context learning, emphasizing the need for a unified evaluation benchmark.
papers.limitation:
The study only compares FVs and ICVs on a relatively small set of functional and behavioral tasks, so results may not generalize to an expanded set of tasks.
The work only considers two steering methods, so findings may not generalize to all bottom-up or top-down approaches for vector steering or interpretability.
future_direction: Expanding the scope of the study to other tasks, models, and steering methods.
Developing explanations for the variable performance of FVs and ICVs to improve understanding of in-context learning in LLMs.
papers.abstract: A key objective of interpretability research on large language models (LLMs) is to develop methods for robustly steering models toward desired behaviors. To this end, two distinct approaches to interpretability -- ``bottom-up" and ``top-down" -- have been presented, but there has been little quantitative comparison between them. We present a case study comparing the effectiveness of representative vector steering methods from each branch: function vectors (FV; arXiv:2310.15213), as a bottom-up method, and in-context vectors (ICV; arXiv:2311.06668) as a top-down method. While both aim to capture compact representations of broad in-context learning tasks, we find they are effective only on specific types of tasks: ICVs outperform FVs in behavioral shifting, whereas FVs excel in tasks requiring more precision. We discuss the implications for future evaluations of steering methods and for further research into top-down and bottom-up steering given these findings.

papers.title: Refusal in LLMs is an Affine Function
papers.research_question: How can affine concept editing (ACE) provide more precise and standardized control over refusal behavior in language models compared to existing steering methods?
papers.core_contribution: ACE unifies directional ablation and activation addition in an affine framework, enabling more standardized and precise control over refusal behavior in language models, and generalizes to models where prior methods fail.
papers.conclusion: ACE offers a more consistent and standardized approach for steering refusal behavior in LLMs, mitigating limitations of existing methods and working across diverse model architectures.
papers.key_findings:
ACE provides more standardized steering than contrastive activation addition (CAA), reducing dependency on input prompts for refusal control.
ACE corrects the issue of nonsense generation in models like Hermes Eagle RWKV v5, where directional ablation alone produces incoherent outputs.
The standardization effect of ACE is not perfect, but parameters slightly below zero and above one are effective for controlling refusal.
ACE works on both transformer-based models (e.g., Llama 3) and recurrent neural networks (e.g., RWKV v5), demonstrating generalizability.
ACE combines affine subspace projection and activation addition to reliably control refusal across different prompt types.
papers.limitation: The standardization effect of ACE is not perfect, suggesting that steering vectors may be flawed or that directional ablation does not fully erase information.
future_direction: Exploring whether nonlinear techniques are required to fully erase concepts like refusal.
Extending steering techniques to work reliably on a more varied set of behaviors.
papers.abstract: We propose affine concept editing (ACE) as an approach for steering language models' behavior by intervening directly in activations. We begin with an affine decomposition of model activation vectors and show that prior methods for steering model behavior correspond to subsets of terms of this decomposition. We then provide a derivation of ACE and use it to control refusal behavior on ten different models, including Llama 3 70B. ACE combines affine subspace projection and activation addition to reliably control the model's refusal responses across prompt types. We evaluate the results using LLM-based scoring on a collection of harmful and harmless prompts. Our experiments demonstrate that ACE consistently achieves more precise control over model behavior than existing methods and generalizes to models where directional ablation via affine subspace projection alone produces incoherent outputs. Code for reproducing our results is available at https://github.com/EleutherAI/steering-llama3 .

papers.title: LatentQA: Teaching LLMs to Decode Activations Into Natural Language
papers.research_question: How can we train a language model to decode activations into natural language answers to open-ended questions about those activations (LATENTQA), and how can this be used for reading and controlling model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces LatentInterpretationTuning (LIT), a method to train a decoder LLM to answer open-ended questions about model activations (LATENTQA), and demonstrates its effectiveness for reading activations and controlling model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that LATENTQA, enabled by LIT, provides a powerful framework for reading and controlling model activations with natural language, and scales well with data and model size.
papers.key_findings:
LIT achieves higher accuracy than GPT-4 and SelfIE in uncovering hidden system prompts.
LIT outperforms linear probing and Patchscope in relational knowledge extraction.
LIT is the only method that significantly reduces bias in the debiasing task.
LIT can steer models to exhibit unseen behaviors (e.g., Golden Gate Claude).
LIT benefits from scaling in dataset and model size.
future_direction: Training LATENTQA systems on additional types of data (e.g., hierarchical instruction-following) to unlock novel applications.
Scaling LATENTQA to larger datasets and models.
Using LATENTQA for evaluating instruction following in long-context scenarios.
papers.abstract: Interpretability methods seek to understand language model representations, yet the outputs of most such methods -- circuits, vectors, scalars -- are not immediately human-interpretable. In response, we introduce LatentQA, the task of answering open-ended questions about model activations in natural language. Towards solving LatentQA, we propose Latent Interpretation Tuning (LIT), which finetunes a decoder LLM on a dataset of activations and associated question-answer pairs, similar to how visual instruction tuning trains on question-answer pairs associated with images. We use the decoder for diverse reading applications, such as extracting relational knowledge from representations or uncovering system prompts governing model behavior. Our decoder also specifies a differentiable loss that we use to control models, such as debiasing models on stereotyped sentences and controlling the sentiment of generations. Finally, we extend LatentQA to reveal harmful model capabilities, such as generating recipes for bioweapons and code for hacking.

papers.title: Local Contrastive Editing of Gender Stereotypes
papers.research_question: How can we localize individual weights that drive stereotypical gender bias in language models and modify these weights to steer and mitigate the bias?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces local contrastive editing, a two-step method to localize and edit a small subset (<0.5%) of model weights that encode gender bias, enabling flexible control and mitigation of bias while largely preserving model performance.
papers.conclusion: Stereotypical gender bias is encoded in specific subsets of weights within language models, and local contrastive editing can effectively identify and modify these subsets to control and mitigate bias.
papers.key_findings:
A very small subset (<0.5%) of model weights is responsible for encoding stereotypical gender bias.
Local contrastive editing strategies (interpolation, extrapolation, pruning) can successfully steer and mitigate gender bias in a controlled manner.
The identified bias-encoding weights are concentrated in higher layers of the transformer, particularly in the attention output dense layer.
Editing based on strategic localization is crucial; uninformed editing of random weights does not effectively change bias.
The method preserves the model's language modeling ability and downstream task performance, except for value-based pruning which degrades performance.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted using a single model architecture (BERT) and a single type of bias (gender bias).
Computational constraints limit the scope of experiments, as iterative magnitude pruning requires substantial resources.
The study uses a binary specification of gender (male/female), which does not encompass the full gender spectrum.
future_direction: Explore application of local contrastive editing to other tasks and domains beyond gender bias.
papers.abstract: Stereotypical bias encoded in language models (LMs) poses a threat to safe language technology, yet our understanding of how bias manifests in the parameters of LMs remains incomplete. We introduce local contrastive editing that enables the localization and editing of a subset of weights in a target model in relation to a reference model. We deploy this approach to identify and modify subsets of weights that are associated with gender stereotypes in LMs. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate that local contrastive editing can precisely localize and control a small subset (< 0.5%) of weights that encode gender bias. Our work (i) advances our understanding of how stereotypical biases can manifest in the parameter space of LMs and (ii) opens up new avenues for developing parameter-efficient strategies for controlling model properties in a contrastive manner.

papers.title: Mechanistic interpretability of large language models with applications to the financial services industry
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be used to understand the inner workings of large language models for financial services applications, specifically for compliance monitoring?
papers.core_contribution: This paper pioneers the application of mechanistic interpretability to financial services, designing algorithmic tasks for compliance monitoring and analyzing GPT-2 Small's attention patterns for identifying potential Fair Lending violations.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability techniques can be successfully applied to understand LLM behavior in financial compliance tasks, providing insights into the roles of specific attention heads and MLP layers.
papers.key_findings:
Heads 11.4, 8.9, and 6.3 contribute positively to the Fair Lending task completion, while heads 0.6, 11.0, and 10.7 contribute negatively.
MLP layers 2 and 4 significantly improve task completion, while MLP layer 10 and attention layer 0 decrease performance.
Activation patching reveals that heads 10.2, 10.7, and 11.3 (positive) and heads 9.6 and 10.6 (negative) play significant roles, with head 10.2's value vector being particularly important.
The Fair Lending compliance task is more complex than the IOI task, involving information processing across many layers rather than being localized to a few final layers.
Value patching has a more significant effect than key or query patching for important heads in later layers (9-11).
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to GPT-2 Small, a relatively small model, and may not generalize to larger, more powerful LLMs.
The financial compliance task is more complex than the IOI task, making circuit discovery more challenging and less localized.
future_direction: Conducting experiments with more powerful open-source LLMs such as Mistral 7B and Llama-2 7B.
Working on more algorithmic examples of compliance tasks in financial services and finding prompts that result in large logit differences.
Performing path patching as a more sophisticated circuit discovery approach for end-to-end circuit identification.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models exhibit remarkable capabilities across a broad spectrum of applications. Nevertheless, due to their intrinsic complexity, these models present substantial challenges in interpreting their internal decision-making processes. This lack of transparency poses critical challenges when it comes to their adaptation by financial institutions, where concerns and accountability regarding bias, fairness, and reliability are of paramount importance. Mechanistic interpretability aims at reverse engineering complex AI models such as transformers. In this paper, we are pioneering the use of mechanistic interpretability to shed some light on the inner workings of large language models for use in financial services applications. We offer several examples of how algorithmic tasks can be designed for compliance monitoring purposes. In particular, we investigate GPT-2 Small’s attention pattern when prompted to identify potential violation of Fair Lending laws. Using direct logit attribution, we study the contributions of each layer and its corresponding attention heads to the logit difference in the residual stream. Finally, we design clean and corrupted prompts and use activation patching as a causal intervention method to localize our task completion components further. We observe that the (positive) heads 10.2 (head 2, layer 10), 10.7, and 11.3, as well as the (negative) heads 9.6 and 10.6 play a significant role in the task completion.

papers.title: Evidence from fMRI Supports a Two-Phase Abstraction Process in Language Models
papers.research_question: Why are intermediate layers of LLMs, rather than output layers, most predictive of brain activity? Is this due to the abstraction/composition process or the next-token prediction objective?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that the similarity between LLM representations and brain activity is driven by the abstraction/composition process within LLMs, not by their next-token prediction objective. This is supported by a strong correlation between layerwise encoding performance and the intrinsic dimensionality of representations.
papers.conclusion: The abstraction process in LLMs, characterized by increasing intrinsic dimensionality in intermediate layers, is supported by evidence from fMRI encoding models and is the primary driver of brain-model similarity, rather than the next-token prediction objective.
papers.key_findings:
Encoding performance for predicting brain activity and the intrinsic dimensionality (Id) of layer representations are highly correlated across layers and model sizes.
A two-phase process exists in LLMs: an early abstraction/composition phase (where Id and encoding performance increase) followed by a later prediction phase (where Id decreases and next-token prediction loss drops sharply).
The peak of encoding performance and Id shifts to earlier layers as training progresses, indicating the abstraction phase becomes more compressed.
The relationship between encoding performance and Id emerges during training and is not a trivial function of architecture or layer index.
Brain regions involved in higher-level linguistic processing show a stronger correlation between encoding performance and Id than low-level auditory cortex.
papers.limitation:
The study only tests two model families (OPT and Pythia), so conclusions may not generalize to all LLMs.
It is inherently challenging to draw affirmative conclusions about underlying brain mechanisms from brain-model similarity alone.
future_direction: Test the findings on more model families to establish generalizability.
Explore methods to combine representations from different layers to create a representation with higher intrinsic dimensionality and potentially better encoding performance.
papers.abstract: Research has repeatedly demonstrated that intermediate hidden states extracted from large language models are able to predict measured brain response to natural language stimuli. Yet, very little is known about the representation properties that enable this high prediction performance. Why is it the intermediate layers, and not the output layers, that are most capable for this unique and highly general transfer task? In this work, we show that evidence from language encoding models in fMRI supports the existence of a two-phase abstraction process within LLMs. We use manifold learning methods to show that this abstraction process naturally arises over the course of training a language model and that the first "composition" phase of this abstraction process is compressed into fewer layers as training continues. Finally, we demonstrate a strong correspondence between layerwise encoding performance and the intrinsic dimensionality of representations from LLMs. We give initial evidence that this correspondence primarily derives from the inherent compositionality of LLMs and not their next-word prediction properties.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Large Language Model Bias Mitigation from the Perspective of Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate social biases in large language models while preserving individual facts and existing knowledge, moving beyond group-level parity?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a fine-grained bias mitigation method (FAST) that calibrates individual biased knowledge while preserving existing knowledge, and establishes a comprehensive debiasing benchmark (BiasKE).
papers.conclusion: Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficacy of FAST, showcasing its generalizability, specificity, and scalability for fine-grained bias mitigation in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
FAST achieves near-perfect bias mitigation (SS close to 50) while maintaining high knowledge preservation (DS).
FAST outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on both bias mitigation and knowledge preservation metrics.
FAST is scalable to larger models like GPT-Neo and Llama-2, though with slightly reduced effectiveness.
FAST maintains general language modeling capability as shown by GLUE scores.
The method locates critical layers responsible for biased predictions and enables editable fairness with lightweight parameters.
papers.limitation:
Requires human-relevant social bias knowledge, which is time-consuming and labor-intensive to collect.
Debiasing performance on larger models is less pronounced due to the complexity of knowledge embedded.
future_direction: Integrate automated social bias detection methods to enhance bias knowledge base construction.
Expand the fairness edit method against attack scenarios.
Improve debiasing effectiveness on larger models.
papers.abstract: Existing debiasing methods inevitably make unreasonable or undesired predictions as they are designated and evaluated to achieve parity across different social groups but leave aside individual facts, resulting in modified existing knowledge. In this paper, we first establish a new bias mitigation benchmark BiasKE leveraging existing and additional constructed datasets, which systematically assesses debiasing performance by complementary metrics on fairness, specificity, and generalization. Meanwhile, we propose a novel debiasing method, Fairness Stamp (FAST), which enables editable fairness through fine-grained calibration on individual biased knowledge. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that FAST surpasses state-of-the-art baselines with remarkable debiasing performance while not hampering overall model capability for knowledge preservation, highlighting the prospect of fine-grained debiasing strategies for editable fairness in LLMs.

papers.title: Quantifying and Mitigating Unimodal Biases in Multimodal Large Language Models: A Causal Perspective
papers.research_question: How do unimodal biases affect Multimodal Large Language Models in Visual Question Answering tasks, and how can they be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a causal framework to interpret unimodal biases in MLLMs, introduces the MORE dataset for evaluation, and develops the CAVE method to mitigate these biases.
papers.conclusion: The causal framework and MORE dataset provide insights into unimodal biases, and CAVE shows promise in enhancing MLLM reasoning, though challenges remain.
papers.key_findings:
MLLMs exhibit strong reliance on unimodal biases and perform poorly on the MORE dataset, not surpassing random baseline.
MLLMs struggle with multi-hop reasoning, especially as complexity increases.
GPT-4v is particularly challenged by GPT-generated distractors in language bias options.
CAVE significantly enhances performance of GPT-4o and Gemini Pro Vision, but absolute accuracy remains low.
papers.limitation:
Rationale generation is based on heuristic rules and could be improved with LLM refinement.
The Wikidata5M dataset may contain outdated information, potentially leading to errors in training data.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have facilitated the development of Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs). Despite their impressive capabilities, MLLMs often suffer from over-reliance on unimodal biases (e.g., language bias and vision bias), leading to incorrect answers or hallucinations in complex multimodal tasks. To investigate this issue, we propose a causal framework to interpret the biases in Visual Question Answering (VQA) problems. Within this framework, we conduct an in-depth causal analysis to assess the causal effect of these biases on MLLM predictions. Based on the analysis, we introduce 1) a novel MORE dataset with 12,000 challenging VQA instances requiring multi-hop reasoning and overcoming unimodal biases. 2) a causality-enhanced agent framework CAVE that guides models to comprehensively integrate information from different modalities and mitigate biases. Our experiments show that MLLMs perform poorly on MORE, indicating strong unimodal biases and limited semantic understanding. However, when integrated with our CAVE, promising improvements in reasoning and bias mitigation can be seen. These findings provide important insights for the development of more robust MLLMs and contribute to the broader goal of advancing multimodal AI systems capable of deeper understanding and reasoning. Our project page is at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/MORE.

papers.title: Toward a Flexible Framework for Linear Representation Hypothesis Using Maximum Likelihood Estimation
papers.research_question: How can we generalize the linear representation hypothesis to handle complex, context-dependent concepts without relying on single-token counterfactual pairs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a generalized framework that redefines binary concepts as unit vectors in a canonical representation space and uses activation differences formalized via a von Mises-Fisher distribution and maximum likelihood estimation to compute concept directions, eliminating the need for single-token counterfactual pairs.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a generalized framework that bridges linear representation hypothesis and representation engineering, offering a principled and robust method for constructing concept directions that is lightweight, flexible, and effective for monitoring and manipulating LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed SAND method consistently outperforms PCA and zero-shot baselines in monitoring truthfulness and other QA tasks across LLaMA models.
SAND accurately captures concept directions (e.g., for gender, case, language) for steering interventions, whereas PCA fails in some cases.
SAND is computationally efficient, requiring only one matrix multiplication, making it lightweight and easy to integrate into existing activation engineering pipelines.
The method provides theoretical justification for the empirical effectiveness of the heuristic Mean Difference method for extracting steering vectors.
The framework bridges the gap between the theory of linear representation hypothesis and the practice of representation engineering.
papers.abstract: Linear representation hypothesis posits that high-level concepts are encoded as linear directions in the representation spaces of LLMs. Park et al. (2024) formalize this notion by unifying multiple interpretations of linear representation, such as 1-dimensional subspace representation and interventions, using a causal inner product. However, their framework relies on single-token counterfactual pairs and cannot handle ambiguous contrasting pairs, limiting its applicability to complex or context-dependent concepts. We introduce a new notion of binary concepts as unit vectors in a canonical representation space, and utilize LLMs' (neural) activation differences along with maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) to compute concept directions (i.e., steering vectors). Our method, Sum of Activation-base Normalized Difference (SAND), formalizes the use of activation differences modeled as samples from a von Mises-Fisher (vMF) distribution, providing a principled approach to derive concept directions. We extend the applicability of Park et al. (2024) by eliminating the dependency on unembedding representations and single-token pairs. Through experiments with LLaMA models across diverse concepts and benchmarks, we demonstrate that our lightweight approach offers greater flexibility, superior performance in activation engineering tasks like monitoring and manipulation.

papers.title: Understanding (Un)Reliability of Steering Vectors in Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the influence of prompt types and the geometry of activation differences on the reliability of steering vectors in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that steering vector reliability depends on the directional consistency of activation differences and the separability of activations along the steering direction, and is unreliable when the target behavior is not represented by a coherent linear direction.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a deeper understanding of when and why steering vectors are (un)reliable, showing that their effectiveness depends on whether the targeted behavior is well-represented as a linear direction in the model’s activation space.
papers.key_findings:
All seven prompt types produce a net positive steering effect but exhibit high variance and often give an effect opposite of the desired one.
No prompt type clearly outperforms the others, and steering vectors from different prompt types often differ directionally.
Higher cosine similarity between training set activation differences predicts more effective steering.
Datasets where positive and negative activations are better separated are more steerable.
Steering vectors are unreliable when the target behavior is not represented by a coherent direction in activation space.
papers.limitation:
Breadth of experiments: only evaluated on Llama2-7B-Chat and 36 multiple-choice datasets, and only focused on CAA; generalizability to other models, datasets, and steering methods is unclear.
Methodology for prompt type comparison is highly sensitive to hyperparameters like training-set size, complicating robust analysis.
future_direction: Investigate different models and non-multiple choice datasets to determine broader generalizability.
Verify transfer of results to other steering vector methods like Function Vectors and BiPO.
Investigate how prompting strategies affect performance on unrelated general benchmarks like MMLU.
papers.abstract: Steering vectors are a lightweight method to control language model behavior by adding a learned bias to the activations at inference time. Although steering demonstrates promising performance, recent work shows that it can be unreliable or even counterproductive in some cases. This paper studies the influence of prompt types and the geometry of activation differences on steering reliability. First, we find that all seven prompt types used in our experiments produce a net positive steering effect, but exhibit high variance across samples, and often give an effect opposite of the desired one. No prompt type clearly outperforms the others, and yet the steering vectors resulting from the different prompt types often differ directionally (as measured by cosine similarity). Second, we show that higher cosine similarity between training set activation differences predicts more effective steering. Finally, we observe that datasets where positive and negative activations are better separated are more steerable. Our results suggest that vector steering is unreliable when the target behavior is not represented by a coherent direction.

papers.title: Computational Basis of LLM's Decision Making in Social Simulation
papers.research_question: How are social meanings internally represented in LLMs, and how can those internal representations be systematically manipulated to steer model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for extracting and manipulating social concept vectors in LLMs' residual streams to steer decision-making in social simulations, specifically demonstrated in a Dictator Game.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a practical bridge between sociological theory and the internal geometry of modern language models, turning LLMs from opaque black boxes into calibrated instruments for theory testing, bounded synthetic data, and auditable interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Social variables like framing (give vs. take) and social distance (stranger meet) significantly affect the LLM's decision to transfer money in the Dictator Game.
These variables are encoded as vectors in the residual stream, and their alignment with the decision vector can be measured via cosine similarity and dot product.
By projecting and injecting these variable vectors into the residual stream, the model's decisions can be steered in a controlled manner.
The steering effect is layer-dependent and can be fine-tuned by adjusting the injection coefficient, with earlier layers having more amplified effects.
The method allows for precise manipulation of specific variables (e.g., gender) without affecting others, enabling targeted interventions.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on internal representational validity and controlled steering within the model's activation space, but does not establish external sociological validity (i.e., correspondence to human cognition and behavior).
The method requires access to the model's internal weights and activations, so it is only feasible with open-weight models.
future_direction: From Scripts to User-Friendly Tools: developing a user-friendly software package to make activation-based steering more accessible.
Expanding to other Social Constructs and Experiments: applying the framework to a wider range of social constructs and experimental paradigms.
Bridging the Gap Between Internal and External Validity: conducting systematic human-LLM comparisons to establish external sociological validity.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as human-like decision-making agents in social science and applied settings. These LLM-agents are typically assigned human-like characters and placed in real-life contexts. However, how these characters and contexts shape an LLM's behavior remains underexplored. This study proposes and tests methods for probing, quantifying, and modifying an LLM's internal representations in a Dictator Game, a classic behavioral experiment on fairness and prosocial behavior. We extract ``vectors of variable variations'' (e.g., ``male'' to ``female'') from the LLM's internal state. Manipulating these vectors during the model's inference can substantially alter how those variables relate to the model's decision-making. This approach offers a principled way to study and regulate how social concepts can be encoded and engineered within transformer-based models, with implications for alignment, debiasing, and designing AI agents for social simulations in both academic and commercial applications, strengthening sociological theory and measurement.

papers.title: Linear socio-demographic representations emerge in Large Language Models from indirect cues
papers.research_question: How do LLMs encode sociodemographic attributes of human conversational partners inferred from indirect cues such as names and occupations, and do these representations shape downstream behavior?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs develop linear representations of user sociodemographic attributes within their activation space from indirect cues, and these representations actively shape downstream behavior, revealing an alignment gap where models refuse explicit demographic queries but act on implicit biases.
papers.conclusion: LLMs linearly encode user demographic attributes from indirect cues, and these representations have measurable behavioral consequences, posing significant challenges for fairness in deployed conversational AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode user sociodemographics in linear subspaces of activation space that can be decoded with high accuracy using linear probes.
Implicit cues such as names and occupations trigger demographic representations aligned with real-world population statistics (e.g., US Census, Bureau of Labor Statistics).
Inference-time interventions (activation steering) demonstrate that these linear representations causally influence model outputs, such as country-of-origin or name predictions.
Models exhibit an alignment gap: commercial models refuse explicit demographic-based reasoning while implicitly encoding and acting upon demographics inferred from contextual cues.
Stereotypical associations in the model's representations correlate with distributional patterns in the training data, as shown for OLMo and Common Crawl.
papers.limitation:
The study uses synthetic prompts designed for experimental control; generalization to organic user interactions is uncertain.
Binary demographic categories (male/female, Black/White, rich/poor) fail to capture the continuous and multidimensional nature of human identity.
The prompts and data sources (US Census, BLS, Kozlowski et al. survey) reflect Western and primarily American cultural framings.
The findings demonstrate correlational patterns between training data, representations, and behavior but do not establish causation.
future_direction: Deeper cross-cultural analysis to understand how biases manifest across different cultural contexts.
Establishing causal relationships between training data, internal representations, and behavioral outputs.
Developing and evaluating intervention techniques (e.g., activation steering, representation debiasing) to mitigate bias without compromising model capabilities.
papers.abstract: We investigate how LLMs encode sociodemographic attributes of human conversational partners inferred from indirect cues such as names and occupations. We show that LLMs develop linear representations of user demographics within activation space, wherein stereotypically associated attributes are encoded along interpretable geometric directions. We first probe residual streams across layers of four open transformer-based LLMs (Magistral 24B, Qwen3 14B, GPT-OSS 20B, OLMo2-1B) prompted with explicit demographic disclosure. We show that the same probes predict demographics from implicit cues: names activate census-aligned gender and race representations, while occupations trigger representations correlated with real-world workforce statistics. These linear representations allow us to explain demographic inferences implicitly formed by LLMs during conversation. We demonstrate that these implicit demographic representations actively shape downstream behavior, such as career recommendations. Our study further highlights that models that pass bias benchmark tests may still harbor and leverage implicit biases, with implications for fairness when applied at scale.

papers.title: FairSteer: Inference Time Debiasing for LLMs with Dynamic Activation Steering
papers.research_question: Can we mitigate bias in LLMs without retraining, instead deferring the debiasing process to the inference stage? Can fairness-related concepts be encoded as separable geometric structures in hidden states, enabling bias mitigation through activation steering?
papers.core_contribution: FairSteer is a novel inference-time debiasing framework that detects bias signatures in model activations using a lightweight linear classifier and applies debiasing steering vectors, computed from contrast prompt pairs, to dynamically adjust activations during inference without retraining.
papers.conclusion: FairSteer is an effective inference-time debiasing method that mitigates bias in LLMs without requiring retraining, demonstrating broad applicability across tasks while preserving model capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Fairness-related features are linearly separable in the hidden activation space of LLMs, with over 90% linear separability in intermediate layers.
FairSteer effectively reduces bias in question-answering, counterfactual input evaluation, and open-ended text generation tasks across six LLMs.
The method preserves the original model performance on general knowledge tasks (MMLU, ARC, OpenBookQA) and language modeling (WikiText 103).
The Biased Activation Detection (BAD) component is crucial for balancing accuracy and bias reduction; using only the Debiasing Steering Vector (DSV) leads to accuracy drops.
Debiasing Steering Vectors (DSVs) computed from contrast prompt pairs are highly similar across different bias categories, indicating a common underlying structure in the activation space.
papers.limitation:
The reliance on a linear classifier may limit its ability to detect more complex, non-linear forms of bias embedded in model activations.
The effectiveness of the debiasing steering vector depends on the quality and representativeness of the biased-unbiased prompt pairs used during its construction, which may not capture all types of bias present in real-world scenarios.
The approach to derive the debiasing steering vector may not be optimal; the work serves primarily as a proof of concept rather than a thorough exploration of the most effective extraction techniques.
While assessed across six open-source models, the generalizability to other models, especially large-scale proprietary systems and future architectures, remains uncertain.
future_direction: Refine and enhance the methodology for deriving debiasing steering vectors.
Explore adaptive scaling of the intervention strength based on the severity of the bias (using classifier confidence scores).
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are prone to capturing biases from training corpus, leading to potential negative social impacts. Existing prompt-based debiasing methods exhibit instability due to their sensitivity to prompt changes, while fine-tuning-based techniques incur substantial computational overhead and catastrophic forgetting. In this paper, we propose FairSteer, a novel inference-time debiasing framework without requiring customized prompt design or model retraining. Motivated by the linear representation hypothesis, our preliminary investigation demonstrates that fairness-related features can be encoded into separable directions in the hidden activation space. FairSteer operates in three steps: biased activation detection, debiasing steering vector (DSV) computation, and dynamic activation steering. Specifically, it first trains a lightweight linear classifier to detect bias signatures in activations, and then computes DSVs as intervention directions derived from small contrastive prompt pairs. Subsequently, it performs debiasing by adjusting activations with DSVs in the inference stage. Comprehensive evaluation with six LLMs demonstrates the superiority of FairSteer across question-answering, counterfactual input evaluation and open-ended text generation tasks. Code will be released.

papers.title: Activation Steering for Bias Mitigation: An Interpretable Approach to Safer LLMs
papers.research_question: Can bias in large language models be detected and mitigated by probing internal activations and applying steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interpretability-based system that uses linear probes to detect bias in LLM activations and applies steering vectors to mitigate biased outputs in real-time.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that bias can be detected and mitigated through activation steering, offering a transparent method for improving LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on internal activations can detect bias with near-perfect accuracy in later layers of gpt2-large.
Bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers, as shown by increasing probe accuracy.
Steering vectors computed from activation differences can successfully alter biased completions toward more neutral alternatives during inference.
The method provides a direct and interpretable approach to bias mitigation without modifying model weights.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted only on gpt2-large, limiting generalizability to other models.
The training dataset is synthetic, which may not fully represent real-world bias.
future_direction: Investigate whether findings generalize to other model architectures and sizes (e.g., Llama, Mistral).
Validate techniques on real-world datasets of hate speech or bias (e.g., HateXplain, CivilComments).
Explore the use of non-linear probes or more sophisticated steering techniques for more precise control.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more integrated into societal systems, the risk of them perpetuating and amplifying harmful biases becomes a critical safety concern. Traditional methods for mitigating bias often rely on data filtering or post-hoc output moderation, which treat the model as an opaque black box. In this work, we introduce a complete, end-to-end system that uses techniques from mechanistic interpretability to both identify and actively mitigate bias directly within a model's internal workings. Our method involves two primary stages. First, we train linear "probes" on the internal activations of a model to detect the latent representations of various biases (e.g., gender, race, age). Our experiments on \texttt{gpt2-large} demonstrate that these probes can identify biased content with near-perfect accuracy, revealing that bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers. Second, we leverage these findings to compute "steering vectors" by contrasting the model's activation patterns for biased and neutral statements. By adding these vectors during inference, we can actively steer the model's generative process away from producing harmful, stereotypical, or biased content in real-time. We demonstrate the efficacy of this activation steering technique, showing that it successfully alters biased completions toward more neutral alternatives. We present our work as a robust and reproducible system that offers a more direct and interpretable approach to building safer and more accountable LLMs.

papers.title: Steering Risk Preferences in Large Language Models by Aligning Behavioral and Neural Representations
papers.research_question: How can steering vectors be systematically identified to change LLM behavior? The paper proposes a principled approach by aligning latent representations from behavioral methods (Markov chain Monte Carlo with LLMs) with neural counterparts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for deriving steering vectors by aligning behavioral representations (elicited via MCMC with LLMs) with neural activations, enabling precise control of LLM risk preferences without retraining.
papers.conclusion: Self-alignment methods that align behavioral and neural representations offer an effective and principled means of controlling LLM behavior in risk-sensitive contexts.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors derived from aligned behavioral and neural representations (MCMC and Certainty Equivalent methods) outperform Contrastive Activation in steering risky decisions, risk perception, and text generation.
The optimal layer for steering varies: risk perception is more steerable in earlier layers, while risky decisions are more steerable in later layers.
The method allows precise control over risk preferences (risk-seeking vs. risk-averse) across different tasks.
Steering vectors transfer to tasks far from the original elicitation context.
The behavioral representation from MCMC reveals more nuanced risk preferences compared to the Certainty Equivalent method.
papers.limitation:
Further theoretical and mechanistic interpretability research is needed to establish a more concrete link between behaviorally elicited representations and their corresponding neural activations.
Modifying a Transformer’s residual stream is not uniformly effective across all layers; the success of such interventions is highly dependent on the layer selected. Identifying optimal layers for steering remains an open question.
This form of steering is limited in scope for proprietary models where weights are not accessible, restricting its broader applicability.
future_direction: Identifying optimal layers for steering remains an open question for future research.
Future research should consider developing new descriptive frameworks tailored to characterizing and predicting the risky choices of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Changing the behavior of large language models (LLMs) can be as straightforward as editing the Transformer's residual streams using appropriately constructed "steering vectors." These modifications to internal neural activations, a form of representation engineering, offer an effective and targeted means of influencing model behavior without retraining or fine-tuning the model. But how can such steering vectors be systematically identified? We propose a principled approach for uncovering steering vectors by aligning latent representations elicited through behavioral methods (specifically, Markov chain Monte Carlo with LLMs) with their neural counterparts. To evaluate this approach, we focus on extracting latent risk preferences from LLMs and steering their risk-related outputs using the aligned representations as steering vectors. We show that the resulting steering vectors successfully and reliably modulate LLM outputs in line with the targeted behavior.

papers.title: Unsupervised Concept Vector Extraction for Bias Control in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we extract concept representations (like gender) from LLMs without labeled data and use them to measure and manipulate bias?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an unsupervised method (WMD) for extracting concept steering vectors from LLMs and a projection-based intervention method for bias mitigation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method is effective for extracting steering vectors and mitigating bias in LLMs, and it generalizes to other protected attributes like race.
papers.key_findings:
The WMD method extracts steering vectors that have higher correlation with gender bias than the difference-in-means method.
The projection-based intervention effectively reduces gender bias in model predictions.
The method generalizes to racial bias.
Steering vectors can be transferred to different tasks (Winogenerated and occupational stereotypes).
Debiasing via steering does not significantly harm general model capabilities (MMLU and IFEVAL).
papers.limitation:
The approach oversimplifies gender as a binary concept and does not account for non-binary identities.
The method may not be applicable when factual gender information is needed in predictions.
future_direction: Expand evaluation to a broader range of tasks.
Adopt a more comprehensive approach that considers intersectionality of gender with other social identities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are known to perpetuate stereotypes and exhibit biases. Various strategies have been proposed to mitigate these biases, but most work studies biases as a black-box problem without considering how concepts are represented within the model. We adapt techniques from representation engineering to study how the concept of "gender" is represented within LLMs. We introduce a new method that extracts concept representations via probability weighting without labeled data and efficiently selects a steering vector for measuring and manipulating the model's representation. We develop a projection-based method that enables precise steering of model predictions and demonstrate its effectiveness in mitigating gender bias in LLMs and show that it also generalizes to racial bias. Our code is available at: https://github.com/hannahxchen/gender-bias-steering

papers.title: Mechanistic Control of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we control large language models by understanding their inner working mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of language models can be leveraged to control their behavior in various applications, such as reducing hallucination, improving instruction stability, and enhancing planning in dialogues.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation shows that mechanistic control is a promising approach for aligning language models, and future work should expand the scope of interpretability and control to more complex behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns an emergent world representation of the Othello board, and this representation can be intervened on to edit the model's perceived world state.
Inference-time intervention (ITI) can elicit more truthful answers from language models by shifting activations along truthful directions found in attention heads.
Instruction drift in long conversations is caused by attention decay, and split-softmax can mitigate this drift by forcing the model to pay more attention to the system prompt.
Dialogue action tokens (DAT) enable better planning in multi-turn dialogues by using a planner to predict action vectors that steer the language model towards long-horizon goals.
papers.abstract: This dissertation talks about mechanistic control of large language models (LLM). The intuition is that, in order to rigorously control large language models, it is beneficial to first understand their inner working mechanisms. Even though a fully mechanistic understanding of language models is far from complete at the time this dissertation is written, I will demonstrate several cases where such understanding provides a useful surface for control. I argue that connecting interpretability to real-life applications--e.g., alignment and safety--offers advantages to the development of both fields. I first position this methodological approach within a broader scientific context, discussing and systematizing the role of interpretability in artificial intelligence research. I then present four intensive case studies, each leveraging certain interpretability insights to control the behavior of language models. The interpretability insights I explored span emergent world representations, representation of internal knowledge, phenomenon of attention decay, and representation of users. The demonstrated effects of control include targeted editing of the world model, reduced hallucination, improved stability of system prompts in long conversations, and better planning in multi-turn dialogue.

papers.title: Shifting Perspectives: Steering Vectors for Robust Bias Mitigation in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can steering vectors effectively mitigate social biases in LLMs, and how do they compare to other bias mitigation methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that steering vectors, applied to model activations at inference time, are a lightweight and effective method for mitigating social biases in LLMs, outperforming prompting and Self-Debias with minimal impact on general model performance.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors offer a plug-and-play, interpretable, and computationally lightweight intervention for bias mitigation, achieving substantial bias reduction with minimal impact on core LLM performance.
papers.key_findings:
Steering vectors achieved average accuracy improvements of 12.8% on BBQ, 8.3% on CLEAR-Bias, and 1% on StereoSet.
Steering vectors outperformed prompting and Self-Debias in all cases, and outperformed fine-tuning in 12 out of 17 evaluations.
Steering vectors had the lowest negative impact on MMLU scores (3.9% decrease) compared to other bias mitigation methods tested.
Steering vectors trained on one bias-specific dataset (BBQ) transferred effectively to other tasks and datasets, demonstrating robustness and generalizability.
Linear separability analysis identified optimal intervention layers (13-14) for applying the steering vectors.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on a 7B parameter model, which may not fully capture emergent abilities related to bias observed in larger models.
MMLU may not capture all aspects of language understanding and reasoning; additional benchmarks would provide a more complete assessment.
future_direction: Explore different contrastive dataset structures for constructing steering vectors.
Investigate multi-dimensional steering by controlling along multiple PCA axes simultaneously.
Study cross-axis interactions (e.g., gender vs. race) to mitigate unintended cross-bias amplification.
Develop adaptive coefficient selection strategies to dynamically adjust steering strength per input.
Apply steering vectors to other forms of harmful behaviors (e.g., toxicity, misinformation) and assess real-world impact.
papers.abstract: We present a novel approach to bias mitigation in large language models (LLMs) by applying steering vectors to modify model activations in forward passes. We compute 8 steering vectors, each corresponding to a different social bias axis, such as age, gender, or race, on a training subset of the BBQ dataset and compare the effectiveness of these to 3 additional bias mitigation methods across 4 datasets. When optimized on the BBQ dataset, our individually tuned steering vectors achieve average improvements of 12.8% on BBQ, 8.3% on CLEAR-Bias, and 1% on StereoSet, and show improvements over prompting and Self-Debias in all cases, and improvements over fine-tuning in 12 out of 17 evaluations. In addition, steering vectors showed the lowest impact on MMLU scores of the four bias mitigation methods tested. The work presents the first systematic investigation of steering vectors for bias mitigation, and we demonstrate that they are a powerful and computationally efficient strategy for reducing bias in LLMs, with broader implications for enhancing AI safety.

papers.title: Linear Personality Probing and Steering in LLMs: A Big Five Study
papers.research_question: Whether linear directions aligned with the Big Five personality traits can be used for probing and steering model behavior in large language models.
papers.core_contribution: Linear directions aligned with Big Five traits are effective for personality probing, but steering is context-dependent, working well in forced-choice tasks but limited in open-ended generation or when prompt context is present.
papers.conclusion: Personality-related signals are embedded in the model's representational geometry, but steering vectors show strong context-dependency and are easily overridden by prompt context.
papers.key_findings:
Linear directions derived from regression align with Big Five traits and generalize to trait-relevant adjectives.
Steering with these vectors reliably shifts responses in forced-choice personality assessments.
Steering effects are overridden by explicit personality cues in the prompt.
Steering has minimal effect in open-ended generation tasks.
Regression-derived directions are more effective than SVD-derived directions for steering.
papers.limitation:
Steering effects are overridden by explicit personality cues in the prompt.
Steering is difficult to measure in open-ended generation where clear evaluation metrics are unavailable.
Aggregation across items and characters may obscure personality signals.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit distinct and consistent personalities that greatly impact trust and engagement. While this means that personality frameworks would be highly valuable tools to characterize and control LLMs' behavior, current approaches remain either costly (post-training) or brittle (prompt engineering). Probing and steering via linear directions has recently emerged as a cheap and efficient alternative. In this paper, we investigate whether linear directions aligned with the Big Five personality traits can be used for probing and steering model behavior. Using Llama 3.3 70B, we generate descriptions of 406 fictional characters and their Big Five trait scores. We then prompt the model with these descriptions and questions from the Alpaca questionnaire, allowing us to sample hidden activations that vary along personality traits in known, quantifiable ways. Using linear regression, we learn a set of per-layer directions in activation space, and test their effectiveness for probing and steering model behavior. Our results suggest that linear directions aligned with trait-scores are effective probes for personality detection, while their steering capabilities strongly depend on context, producing reliable effects in forced-choice tasks but limited influence in open-ended generation or when additional context is present in the prompt.

papers.title: How Do LLMs Persuade? Linear Probes Can Uncover Persuasion Dynamics in Multi-Turn Conversations
papers.research_question: How do LLMs persuade in multi-turn conversations? The paper investigates using linear probes to uncover persuasion dynamics, including persuasion success, persuadee personality, and persuasion strategy.
